articles.title: I deleted the mail server from my VPS and got 1.2 GB of RAM back
articles.description: So I run ExtraTime, it's a football trivia site with daily puzzles, the Grid game, multiplayer rooms...
articles.body_html:
So I run ExtraTime, it's a football trivia site with daily puzzles, the Grid game, multiplayer rooms and leaderboards and so on. Backend is Django on one VPS with 8 GB RAM, frontend is Next.js on Vercel. Pretty normal side project setup that kind of grew bigger than I planned.

Until this October the same VPS was also running my own mail server, and I want to write down how I moved off it to smtpfa.st, because honestly it went way better than I expected, and the part where stuff broke was actually the best part (I'll explain).

Nobody asked me to write this post. I'm writing it because I think how it went is worth sharing with other people who self-host their mail without really needing to.

How it was before

When I started I thought email is something I should just own myself, how hard can it be? So I put docker-mailserver in a container next to the app, then a SnappyMail container on top so I can read admin@ from the browser, and then a whole separate git repo only for the mail config. Django sent through it on port 587.

It worked, mostly. But when I actually looked inside the container this October it was running Postfix, Dovecot, rspamd for spam, ClamAV for viruses (just the signature database was 309 MB on disk), and fail2ban because ports 25, 587 and 993 were open to the internet and the bots found them quickly. All of this so my site can send password reset emails and verification links to people, which is the most basic thing an app does.

docker stats showed the mailserver using 1.14 GiB. The same box runs Postgres, Redis, gunicorn, daphne for the websockets, Prometheus and some exporters, so 1.14 GiB for a thing that does nothing most of the day felt wasteful. Early October I was looking where to free some memory and the first idea was to turn ClamAV off, and then I thought, if I'm touching the mail server anyway why not just remove the whole thing and use a proper service.

The RAM was honestly not even the main problem for me. The main problem was I had zero visibility, if a reset email didn't arrive I had no idea if it went to spam or bounced or the address was fake or what. There was no dashboard, no events, nothing I could connect Django to. DMARC was on p=none and the reports were going to a mailbox that I almost never opened.

Plus I wanted to start a newsletter, and sending a newsletter from your own Postfix on a VPS IP address is a pretty good way to get that IP on a blocklist.

Account emails first

This part was boring, in a good way.

smtpfa.st has an SMTP relay so for Django it's only settings, and the password is an API key that can only send:

EMAIL_HOST = "smtp.smtpfa.st"
EMAIL_PORT = 587
EMAIL_USE_TLS = True
EMAIL_HOST_USER = "smtpfast"
EMAIL_HOST_PASSWORD = env("EMAIL_HOST_PASSWORD")  # send-only key

I added their DNS records in Cloudflare, the dashboard showed everything verified, I sent a password reset to myself and it was there in Gmail and in the smtpfa.st logs. That was it.

One thing I didn't know: smtpfa.st treats mail that comes over SMTP as marketing by default, unless you say it isn't. Makes sense because they add the unsubscribe headers and respect opt-outs, but a password reset obviously has to arrive even if the person unsubscribed from the newsletter. There is a header for this, so I made a small email backend that puts it on every email Django sends:

from django.core.mail.backends.smtp import EmailBackend

CATEGORY_HEADER = "X-SMTPfast-Category"
UNTRACKED_HEADERS = {
    "X-SMTPfast-Track-Clicks": "false",
    "X-SMTPfast-Track-Opens": "false",
}


class TransactionalEmailBackend(EmailBackend):
    def send_messages(self, email_messages):
        for message in email_messages or ():
            message.extra_headers.setdefault(CATEGORY_HEADER, "transactional")
            for header, value in UNTRACKED_HEADERS.items():
                message.extra_headers.setdefault(header, value)
        return super().send_messages(email_messages)

They read the headers and remove them before sending. The two tracking headers I added a few days later, there's a story behind those further down.

The newsletter

This is really why I did the whole thing. ExtraTime has around 2,200 registered players from the last few years and I had literally no way to tell them when we add something new, except a banner on the site that only people already on the site will see.

What I ended up with: Django is the source of truth for consent. You turn product emails on or off in your profile and a nightly job syncs that to the contacts in smtpfa.st, and if they ever disagree Django wins. The email templates are React Email in the frontend repo with the same Tailwind colours as the site, a build step turns them to HTML and uploads them as hosted templates, so the emails actually look like ExtraTime and not like some generic template.

Broadcasts I create with the REST API. When we launched country variations for the Grid I didn't want people in Brazil getting the email at 4 in the morning, so the audience got split by country and time zone, which ended up being 18 scheduled broadcasts for one campaign (a bit much, in hindsight). Now I do one batch per day at 10:00 Sofia time and it's much simpler.

Unsubscribes, spam complaints and bounces come back to Django as webhooks, signed with HMAC-SHA256, so verifying is short:

def signature_is_valid(body, header):
    secret = settings.SMTPFAST_WEBHOOK_SECRET
    if not secret or not header:
        return False
    expected = hmac.new(secret.encode(), body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    received = header.strip().removeprefix("sha256=")
    return hmac.compare_digest(expected.encode(), received.encode("utf-8", "replace"))

Every event is saved by its id first so if they retry it nothing happens twice. And for people without an account there's a hosted sign-up form with double opt-in, the /newsletter page on our site posts straight to it and smtpfa.st sends the confirmation mail.

I built most of this with Claude Code, and smtpfa.st has an MCP server and a skill file for agents, which helped more than I thought it would, because the agent was reading the real API response shapes and not guessing them.

Bounces (my fault, not theirs)

First campaign I sent to everyone who was opted in, and a lot of them had not logged in for years. The bounce rate went to 3.9%, and sending gets paused at 5%, and soft bounces count too, not only hard ones. Not a fun number to watch climb.

But this was entirely on me. smtpfa.st showed exactly which addresses bounced and the reason, mostly typos and dead domains from old signups. After that I made a rule that any address that bounces even once never gets mailed again, and we check the MX records too so dead domains get removed before the first send. If you are about to email an old user list for the first time, clean it first.

When stuff broke

This is the part that made me want to write all this.

On October 10, the first day, I hit a bunch of small problems while building everything above, so I wrote them all down and sent them to smtpfa.st support. The same evening I got a reply that started with "Everything you reported is fixed and live now" and a list. Marketing and transactional mail got split, so an unsubscribe doesn't block password resets anymore (that's where the header above comes from). Suppressions now show the reason why an address is blocked. There was a paging bug where contacts in a segment could repeat or disappear because the sort had no tiebreaker, fixed. Tags started coming back on GET /v1/emails/:id, and the docs got the real webhook payloads and bounce types.

Next morning two more things were live, send_over_minutes for spreading a broadcast over a few hours, and custom link domains so the tracking and unsubscribe links use your own hostname. I added one CNAME for a subdomain of extratime.world and the certificate just appeared on its own.

On the 12th I noticed the links inside password reset emails were going through the click tracker. Those links have single-use tokens in them and I really didn't like that they pass through a redirect, so I asked if I can turn tracking off for single emails. First answer was that none of the options exist yet but they will add them. Second answer came the same afternoon and all four were live: SMTP headers, API fields, an account switch for transactional mail, and an attribute for single links. That's the X-SMTPfast-Track-* thing in my backend.

After that I started reporting things as GitHub issues, and the timestamps tell the story better than I can:

Issue Opened Fix PR Closed
#841 Contacts stat boxes weren't clickable filters Oct 14, 07:56 UTC 23 min later ~3 h
#842 No way to archive sent broadcasts Oct 14, 07:59 UTC ~1.5 h later ~3 h
#853 MCP OAuth rejected Claude Code's localhost callback Oct 16, 08:50 UTC 10 min later 20 min

853 is my favourite. Claude Code uses a random localhost port for the OAuth callback and their server only accepted the exact redirect that was registered, so connecting failed. I opened the issue and it was fixed 20 minutes later.

I've worked with the big email providers before and you know how that goes, ticket, auto-reply, and after a week someone says it's on the roadmap. This was nothing like that.

Removing the old server

When everything was going through smtpfa.st, removing the old mail server was quick. I backed up the two mailboxes (less than 200 KB each, which tells you how much I actually used them), stopped and deleted the mailserver and SnappyMail containers, closed 25, 587 and 993 in the firewall, removed the VPS IP from the SPF record, and pointed MX to Cloudflare Email Routing which forwards everything to my Gmail.

Used RAM went from 5,537 MB to 4,322 MB. And it's one repo less, three ports less, and no more ClamAV updating its signatures in the middle of the night for an inbox nobody reads.

So would I recommend it

Yes. It's a young service and in the first weeks you could tell: when I started only the CLI was public, and the dashboard had some rough spots, two of which are in the table above. That moved fast too. There are now official SDKs for Node, Python, Go and PHP, plus a Laravel package and a Terraform provider. But the sending, the webhooks and the docs have been solid for me, and I have never had a provider fix things this fast.

If you are still running Postfix next to your app only for password resets, you probably don't need to.

And if you like football come play the daily Grid on ExtraTime. The newsletter will tell you when there's something new, and this time I can actually see if it arrived.

articles.title: 5 Best Open-source LLM Gateways 💎
articles.description: TL;DR    An open-source LLM gateway gives applications one place to connect to model...
articles.body_html:
TL;DR

  • An open-source LLM gateway gives applications one place to connect to model providers. Depending on the project, it can also handle routing, retries, budgets, access controls, caching and request logs.
  • The five projects here take different approaches: Bifrost, Kong, Agent Router, Apache APISIX and LiteLLM.
  • Bifrost is our pick for teams that want a self-hosted gateway with model, MCP and agent traffic controls. Its commercial Edge product can also route AI traffic from employee devices.
  • Open source does not mean every feature is free or self-hostable. Check each project's license and feature boundaries before adopting it.

A few years ago, many teams adopted gateways to centralize provider keys and billing. Those needs have not gone away, but teams now also have to think about model choice, reliability, usage limits and the growing number of tools connected to agents.

The projects in this list are not interchangeable. Some focus on model routing, while others build AI features on top of a broader API or service-mesh stack. I compared five open-source LLM gateways, their deployment models and the features available without a paid plan.

What an open-source LLM gateway does

At a basic level, an open-source LLM gateway is a reverse proxy for model requests. An application sends traffic to a shared endpoint, and the gateway handles provider-specific formats, routing and retries across services such as OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS Bedrock and Google Vertex AI.

Some projects add budgets, access controls, audit trails, caching or MCP support. Others focus on getting requests to the right model with low operational overhead. The right choice depends on which of those jobs you need the gateway to do.

How to choose an open-source LLM gateway

  • Provider coverage. Confirm the providers and API formats your application needs today, then check how new providers are added.
  • Reliability and latency. Look for retries, fallbacks and load balancing. Treat benchmark numbers as a starting point.
  • Deployment and license. Check the license for the gateway itself, and distinguish open-source components from paid hosting, support or enterprise features.
  • Operations. Consider how the project handles secrets, budgets, access controls, logs and upgrades. A gateway still needs someone to run it.
  • MCP and agent support. If your applications call tools, check whether the gateway routes or governs MCP traffic, and how identity and permissions work.

The five gateways at a glance

Here is the short version. Bifrost and LiteLLM are model-focused gateways, Kong brings AI traffic into a broader API platform, Agent Router is built around Envoy Gateway and Kubernetes, and Apache APISIX combines AI plugins with a general-purpose API gateway. These five open-source LLM gateways differ in deployment and feature boundaries.

Capability Bifrost Kong AI Gateway Agent Router Apache APISIX LiteLLM
Form factor Standalone Go gateway AI features in Kong Gateway Envoy Gateway control plane and CLI API gateway with AI plugins Python SDK and proxy
Model coverage 25+ providers, 10,000+ models Major hosted and self-hosted APIs Hosted and self-hosted providers OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock and more 100+ providers
Routing and reliability Retries, fallbacks, load balancing Routing, load balancing, plugins Central routing, quotas and failover Multi-provider proxy, balancing and retries Routing, retries, fallbacks
MCP support Native MCP gateway AI MCP Proxy plugins AI and MCP traffic OpenAPI-to-MCP plugin MCP gateway
Deployment Self-hosted; Enterprise adds private options Self-hosted or Konnect Kubernetes or standalone CLI Self-hosted Self-hosted proxy
A good fit when You want one gateway for models and agents Kong already runs your APIs Your platform is built on Envoy You want an open-source API and AI gateway Your stack is Python-first

The sections below look at what each project does well, where it fits and what to check before adopting it.

1. Bifrost: A gateway for models, MCP and agents

Bifrost is an open-source LLM gateway for enterprise AI, licensed under Apache 2.0 and written in Go. It provides one OpenAI-compatible interface to more than 10,000 models across 25+ providers. With its drop-in setup, an existing app can usually switch over by changing its base URL. Bifrost ships as a single binary and can run on a VM, in Kubernetes, in a private cloud or on a disconnected network.

Core capabilities

Performance is one of Bifrost's main selling points. Its published benchmarks report about 11 microseconds of overhead at 5,000 requests per second on a single t3.xlarge, with a 100% success rate. In a separate AWS EC2 comparison with 500 concurrent users over 60 seconds, Bifrost handled 424 requests per second, while LiteLLM handled 44.84. The reported P99 latencies were 1.68 seconds and 90.72 seconds, respectively.

For governance, virtual keys let teams set budgets and rate limits by key, team, customer or model. The Enterprise tier connects to identity providers such as Okta, Microsoft Entra, Keycloak, Zitadel, Auth0 and Google Workspace, as well as other OIDC providers. It also adds SCIM 2.0 directory sync, detailed role-based access control, data access controls and reusable access profiles. Routing supports weighted load balancing, retries with backoff and automatic fallbacks. Semantic caching, backed by Redis, Qdrant, Weaviate or Pinecone, can return stored answers for similar prompts.

The MCP gateway controls which MCP servers and tools agents can use. Access can be filtered at the client, request and virtual-key levels, with per-user OAuth so each person connects using their own account. Code Mode takes a different approach to large tool sets: instead of loading every tool definition into the model context, the model writes a short script to coordinate the tools it needs. Bifrost reports that this can reduce input token use by up to 92.8%. In a 508-tool test, the reported cost fell from $377 to $29, with all tasks passing. The MCP gateway write-up has the full results.

Bifrost Edge extends those controls to AI tools running on employee devices. Available for macOS, Windows and Linux, it routes traffic from desktop chat apps, browser-based AI, terminal coding agents and their MCP servers through the Bifrost gateway after a one-time SSO sign-in. Edge routes AI traffic only and does not inspect other device activity. Gateway virtual keys, budgets and guardrails can then apply to those tools, including content safety, PII and secret detection on requests and responses, as well as integrations with AWS Bedrock Guardrails, Azure Content Safety, Google Model Armor, CrowdStrike AIDR and Check Point Guard. Administrators can allow or block apps and MCP servers centrally. Rules are enforced on the device. Rollout can use existing device management tools such as Jamf, Intune, Kandji, Omnissa Workspace ONE or JumpCloud.

For regulated environments, the Enterprise tier adds clustering, adaptive load balancing with circuit breakers, signed audit logs, and integrations with AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager and HashiCorp Vault. It also supports in-VPC, on-premises and air-gapped deployments, where prompts and responses can stay within your infrastructure. Bifrost lists SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, HIPAA and GDPR among its compliance credentials, and says Fortune 500 companies use the product in production across several industries.

Where it fits

There are a few things to check before committing. Identity-based governance, clustering, adaptive load balancing, guardrail and vault integrations, and in-VPC deployment are part of the paid Enterprise tier, not the open-source core. Edge also requires an Enterprise gateway and is priced per endpoint. Since it is still in early access, a limited pilot makes sense before a wider rollout.

Best for: Teams that need to manage model, MCP and agent traffic from one gateway, especially when they have strict deployment or governance requirements. Bifrost supports self-hosted, VPC-isolated, on-premises and air-gapped environments.

💎 Check out the Bifrost repository ☆

2. Kong AI Gateway: AI features in an established API platform

Kong AI Gateway adds AI-specific features to Kong's established API gateway. If your APIs already run on Kong, you can use the same control plane, plugin model and operational setup for model traffic. The AI features include provider routing, token-based rate limits, prompt guard plugins, semantic caching and semantic routing across models.

Core capabilities

Kong added MCP support in Gateway 3.12 in October 2025. Its AI MCP Proxy plugin can expose REST APIs as MCP tools or sit in front of an MCP server. Access controls apply both when clients discover tools and when they invoke them. A companion OAuth2 plugin handles authentication for MCP traffic.

Where it fits

The main trade-offs are licensing and operational scope. Kong's documentation lists the MCP plugins as part of its AI Gateway Enterprise offering, and labels the OAuth2 plugin as a tech preview. If Kong is not already in your stack, deploying the full API gateway platform just for model traffic may be more than you need.

Best for: Organizations that already use Kong and want to manage AI traffic through their existing control plane.

3. Agent Router: Envoy-based routing for Kubernetes

Agent Router, formerly Envoy AI Gateway, is an Apache 2.0 project for managing access to hosted models, self-hosted inference and MCP servers. It provides an OpenAI-compatible API and is built around Envoy Gateway. The repository has moved to theagentrouter, but project documentation says the API resources, API group, CLI name and image paths remain unchanged.

Core capabilities

The project describes a two-tier pattern: one gateway handles shared authentication, routing and global limits, while another can manage traffic to self-hosted inference. It also offers a standalone CLI for local use, which makes it possible to try the API before deploying the Kubernetes components.

Where it fits

The trade-off is its platform focus. Teams already operating Envoy Gateway and Kubernetes have a clear path to evaluate it. For a small application that just needs a lightweight proxy, a simpler gateway may involve less setup. Its documentation and release notes are the best places to check the current status of specific providers and features.

Best for: Platform teams using Envoy Gateway or Kubernetes that want an open-source control plane for model and tool traffic.

4. Apache APISIX: Open-source AI plugins in an API gateway

Core capabilities

Apache APISIX is an Apache Software Foundation project licensed under Apache 2.0. Its open-source API gateway includes AI plugins for connecting to model providers, routing requests across instances, balancing traffic, retrying failures and limiting usage by tokens. The ai-proxy plugin supports documented providers and OpenAI-compatible APIs, while ai-proxy-multi adds multi-instance load balancing and fallback behavior. The ai-rate-limiting plugin applies token quotas.

APISIX also has an openapi-to-mcp plugin that exposes operations from an OpenAPI document as MCP tools. This is a useful contrast with Kong: APISIX's AI plugins are part of its open-source project, while Kong documents its MCP Proxy plugins as Enterprise features.

Where it fits

Because APISIX is a full API gateway, teams adopting it for AI traffic also take on its broader gateway configuration and operations. Its plugin model suits teams that want to manage API and model traffic together, with the AI capabilities available in the open-source project.

Best for: Platform teams that want an open-source API and AI gateway with multi-provider routing, token limits and MCP support.

5. LiteLLM: Broad provider support and a Python-first workflow

Core capabilities

LiteLLM is a common starting point for teams building with language models. It combines an MIT-licensed Python SDK with a self-hosted proxy that supports more than 100 providers, virtual keys, budgets, routing, fallbacks, guardrails and an MCP gateway. Semantic caching supports Qdrant, Valkey and Redis. Its documentation recommends using that feature for single-shot prompts rather than multi-turn agent traffic. A paid enterprise license adds SCIM, audit logs and some guardrail integrations. Admin UI SSO is free for up to five users.

Trade-offs

Two considerations are worth a closer look. In Bifrost's published benchmarks, LiteLLM handled 44.84 requests per second with a P99 latency of 90.72 seconds in an AWS EC2 test with 500 concurrent users over 60 seconds. Bifrost handled 424 requests per second with a P99 latency of 1.68 seconds in the same comparison. These are vendor-published results; performance varies by workload.

There was also a supply-chain incident. Malicious PyPI versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 were published on March 24, 2026; LiteLLM says a maintainer's PyPI account may have been compromised, according to its security update. The affected versions were removed. The incident involved a compromised package release rather than a vulnerability in LiteLLM's gateway code, and highlights the value of pinning dependencies and mirroring packages internally.

Best for: Python-focused teams with moderate traffic that value a broad provider ecosystem and can operate and secure a self-hosted service.

Deployment and licensing compared

This table is a starting point, not a substitute for checking the current license and feature matrix. Several projects keep parts of their enterprise functionality outside the open-source gateway.

Control Bifrost Kong AI Gateway Agent Router Apache APISIX LiteLLM
License Apache 2.0 core; Enterprise features are paid Apache 2.0 Kong Gateway; some AI plugins are paid Apache 2.0 Apache 2.0 MIT core; some enterprise features are paid
Where it runs Self-hosted; private deployment options in Enterprise Self-hosted, hybrid or Konnect Kubernetes or standalone CLI Self-hosted Self-hosted proxy
Main trade-off Some governance and deployment features require Enterprise Advanced AI features may require a license Best suited to Envoy and Kubernetes stacks Broader API gateway to configure and operate Python-based operations and security upkeep

Which AI Gateway Is Right for Your Team

If you are choosing a gateway for production, start with the constraints that matter most to your team. Bifrost provides multi-provider routing, agent workflows and private deployment options. Its published benchmark reports 11 µs of overhead.

LiteLLM is a natural option for Python-centric teams. Kong fits organizations already running Kong, while Agent Router suits teams built around Envoy Gateway and Kubernetes. Apache APISIX adds AI capabilities to an open-source API gateway. The best choice is the one that fits your existing platform and the amount of gateway operations your team is ready to own.

Frequently asked questions

What is an open-source LLM gateway?

An open-source LLM gateway sits between an application and one or more model providers. Depending on the project, it can provide a shared API, route requests, retry failures, apply usage limits and log traffic. Check the license and feature list because commercial hosting or enterprise controls may be separate.

How is an LLM gateway different from an API gateway?

A traditional API gateway focuses on routing and authentication for general API traffic. An LLM gateway adds features specific to model requests, such as provider routing, token-based limits, model fallbacks and usage reporting. Some API gateways now offer AI plugins as well, so the distinction depends on the product.

Should we self-host or use a managed gateway?

Self-hosting gives your team more control over prompts, keys and logs, but also means operating the service. A managed gateway can be quicker to adopt, though traffic passes through the vendor's network. The right choice depends on your security requirements and the operational support available to your team.

Do LLM gateways support MCP?

MCP support varies. Bifrost has a native MCP gateway, Kong offers AI MCP Proxy plugins, Agent Router handles AI and MCP traffic, Apache APISIX provides an openapi-to-mcp plugin, and LiteLLM includes MCP support in its proxy. Compare authentication and tool-level permissions rather than treating support as a yes-or-no feature.

How much latency does an LLM gateway add?

The answer depends on the gateway, workload and enabled features. Bifrost reports about 11 microseconds of overhead at 5,000 requests per second on a single t3.xlarge in its published benchmarks. That is small next to the time many models take to respond, but added latency can matter when an agent makes a long sequence of calls.

Can we move off LiteLLM without rewriting code?

Often, yes. Both products expose OpenAI-compatible APIs, and Bifrost provides drop-in adapters for the LiteLLM SDK. Teams using the LiteLLM proxy can also migrate models, keys, teams and users. See the LiteLLM migration guide for the process and its details.

Can an LLM gateway govern employees using ChatGPT or Claude desktop apps?

Only when that traffic passes through the gateway. A standard gateway typically sees requests that developers have configured to use it. Bifrost Edge is designed to route traffic from desktop apps, browsers and coding agents through Bifrost so gateway policies can apply.

Is Bifrost open source, and what does the Enterprise tier add?

Bifrost's core is open source under Apache 2.0 and can be self-hosted for free. The Enterprise tier adds high availability, identity-based governance, guardrail and vault integrations, signed audit logs, and in-VPC or air-gapped deployment. It includes a 14-day free trial. Bifrost Edge requires an Enterprise gateway and is priced per endpoint.

Conclusion

There is no single gateway that is right for every stack. Choose based on the providers you use, how you plan to deploy, and whether you want a dedicated model proxy or AI features inside an existing API platform. Check which features are included in each open-source project, and test each of the five gateways with your own workload before committing. If Bifrost is on your shortlist, its documentation and demo cover its deployment and Enterprise options.

Resources:

  • Bifrost GitHub: https://github.com/maximhq/bifrost
  • Bifrost Docs: https://docs.getbifrost.ai
  • Bifrost CLI: npx -y @maximhq/bifrost-cli

Thanks for reading this article! ❤️

I'd love to hear your thoughts on this in the comments!

💎 Check out the Bifrost repository ☆

articles.title: 🏢 Ever Fluorescent: Project Plan and Debrief
articles.description: This is going to cover a lot, and I will do my best to keep it brief. Thank you for following the...
articles.body_html:
This is going to cover a lot, and I will do my best to keep it brief. Thank you for following the journey of an independent artist powering through the web. Small, but mighty. ⚡

Last night I had one of those nights where my brain just refused to shut off, despite being tired. This is pretty rare for me, I like the peace that comes with sleeping, and the bed can be a very strong magnet.

Before I fell asleep, I decided I was a project manager, and that my entire strategy needed a facelift.

As solo developer, I leaned into claude to sort out my 9,000 thoughts.

🏹 Strengths: Creativity, drive, ideas, writing, communication, time management, learning, technical skills, inspiring others, general management, and life administration.

⬇️ Weaknesses: Deviating from plans, emotions, self doubt, and other anxieties

👾 Claudinarian

Something clicked in my brain last night. I thought to myself: “This project is so vast that I need A project manager and another developer so that I can run things.” 🤣I sat with that idea for a bit, feeling overwhelmed. I gave some thought to what my real issues were on a very deep and personal level. I reflected on my own existence.

I decided to organize my thoughts with Claude, as is my go-to. I have become quite the claudinarian. Having messed with the “Projects” feature of claude before, the multi-agent bot with an orchestrator at the top, I knew the most appropriate manner to share my thoughts. I had previously gotten lost with this feature in the sub-bots and frequently lost my place and it was very confusing. Having that experience I knew I had to approach claude with targeted, specific and detailed requests. This way, claude would send a minion to do the bidding. Once that started, I could return to claude boss to place a new request. I think I’ve got it figured out now, I won't navigate to a minion and try to complete a project from a sub-agent (Guilty!)

As each task completed, I had Claude build me and artifact for that area of focus. I was creating and collecting organized documentation for myself so I could build a legitimate project plan with enough work to keep me busy for literally weeks.

How it started

The original plan was to optimize SEO, after having been absolutely devastated by my website performance (yes, I felt like a failure for a second “wow, how do I suck that bad? I try so hard!”) 😂

In my previous post, I shared a redirect disaster created from years of doing things on the web for my business as a non-developer. I had made a giant mess for myself. I’m sure if I went to a 'professional' they would have said something like “Here is the rebranding plan for your new business…” not wanting to deal with my disaster. Good thing I started learning web development a few years ago! I have gained so many skills that will be useful for running my small business. Monumentally powerful and not something that too many CEOs can say they can do themselves. Maniacal Laughter

Side tangent again. 😂 pivot Too many redirects in my brain.

First Task

SO, I have boss claude and the minion claudettes doing some legwork. This is my team for the night. Before I created the first task, I did some personal research. After fixing the redirect problem, I investigated my accessibility features to keep it clean. (I had recently completed a formal webdev class and the accessibility stuff was fresh in my head). everfluorescent.com came out mostly good, but I created a To-Do list and added that to it. No big deal, I can handle that.

With redirects created properly, canonical set as it should be and a decent user-friendliness score, I proceeded to run everfluorescent.com through multiple SEO checkers. They returned mixed results as expected. Here is some free ones I used that you may find useful:

  • SEOptimizer (Full audit)
  • Open Graph Preview Tool (Found no share image)
  • SEObility.net (Came back with on-page score of 87%)
  • SavageAudit (85/100 overall - details locked)

Savage Audit is awesome even on the free tier. Look what it said 🤣

I fed claude the data from all 4 sources, I told it to use it as a reference to build my plan.

This morning, I still had a bajillion tabs open and I noticed something. Before implementing the next wave of SEO optimization (not the first time I’m doing this), my average rank in searches was at position 5.3. 5.3!!!! That’s the first page of a Google Search! Boss.

My indexing is currently being fixed as well. As you can see from the chart below, the trends are now moving in the right direction. Redirects improving, proper canonical tag, and 404s have trended downward as well. This is excellent news.

Second Task

Diving into the problem of reach is next. This is something that I am not surprised about. Due to personal reasons, I had basically ghosted all of my social medias for the last few years. I will use an external free tool for scheduled content posting. 24 hours of evidence!

Things are looking up, and we are getting back on the right track. I've still got a monumental amount of work to do, but one thing at a time. I don't want to get excited over some 'blip anomaly' and I'm going to watch it like an obsessed hawk for a while.

articles.title: The Most Embarrassing Private Key in Web PKI History
articles.description: The strange thing about this incident is that the certificates looked normal.  They had familiar CA...
articles.body_html:
The strange thing about this incident is that the certificates looked normal.

They had familiar CA names. They chained to trusted roots. Browsers could validate them. Audit cycles came and went.

But eight eMudhra intermediate certificates had a private key problem so severe that it did not need a supercomputer, a quantum breakthrough, or a clever cryptographic attack.

The private key could be recovered by counting.

That is the story behind the eMudhra CA incident. It is a cryptography failure, but it is also an operational failure, a review failure, and an incident-handling failure.

The public picture is still incomplete. eMudhra has said its final root-cause analysis is still in progress, so this article separates confirmed facts from the likely failure chain described in public reporting.

The short version

On April 30, 2025, a key-generation ceremony produced weak private keys for eight intermediate certificate authorities operated by eMudhra.

The affected certificates used elliptic-curve cryptography. A secure P-384 private key should be a huge random number. The affected values were reportedly below 256. One widely discussed example was a key with the value 4.

That is not “a little weak.” It is equivalent to leaving a four-digit-looking combination lock on a vault that was supposed to have hundreds of digits of randomness.

The public certificates contained the matching public keys. Anyone could take the public key, try the small possible private values, and recover the private key in under a second.

The weak intermediates were publicly trusted for about 18 months. A researcher reported the issue to the Chrome Root Program on October 17, 2026. Chrome and Firefox blocked the affected certificates quickly. eMudhra revoked the intermediates and later announced customer migration support.

No public evidence currently shows that the weak keys were exploited before disclosure. That is good news. It does not make the incident small.

First, what does an intermediate CA actually do?

Most people meet certificate authorities only when a browser shows a padlock. Behind that padlock is a chain of trust.

Trusted root CA
      ↓ signs
Intermediate CA
      ↓ signs
Website or code-signing certificate
      ↓
Browser, device, or application accepts the certificate

The root CA is the high-value trust anchor. Browsers and operating systems keep it in a root store. The root normally stays protected and signs intermediate CAs instead of signing every website certificate itself.

The intermediate CA is the day-to-day issuer. It can sign certificates for websites, software publishers, and other use cases allowed by its constraints.

That is why an intermediate private key matters so much. If an attacker has it, they may be able to create certificates that look legitimate to software that trusts the chain.

This is not about compromising one website. It is about compromising a machine that can make many websites or signed programs look trustworthy.

Why the key being “4” changes everything

For an elliptic-curve key, the public key is calculated from the private key using this relationship:

Q = d × G

Where:

  • d is the private key
  • G is a public, fixed base point for the curve
  • Q is the public key placed in the certificate

With a normal P-384 key, d should be a random value with roughly 384 bits of entropy. The point of elliptic-curve cryptography is that, given a normal public key Q, working backward to find d is infeasible.

But that promise has a condition: the private key has to be random and huge.

If d is less than 256, an attacker does not need to solve a hard math problem. They can calculate:

1 × G
2 × G
3 × G
4 × G
...
255 × G

Then they compare each result to the public key in the certificate. The match reveals the private key.

This is why the failure is so startling. The cryptographic algorithm did not suddenly become weak. The key generation process supplied it with a private value so small that the algorithm never had a chance to provide security.

What public reporting says went wrong

The public account points to a stacked failure, not a single accidental click.

According to eMudhra’s statements and public incident discussions:

  1. The ceremony was intended to generate proper RSA-4096 and P-384 key pairs for a set of intermediates.
  2. A ceremony deviation introduced a wrap-and-unwrap test for HSM key handling.
  3. A flaw in the ceremony script produced a second set of weak EC keys alongside the expected keys.
  4. The weak and strong key sets were labelled similarly.
  5. The wrong key objects were selected when certificate-signing requests were created.
  6. The resulting weak public keys were signed into intermediate CA certificates and cross-signed for compatibility.
  7. The strong keys remained on the HSM but were not the keys represented by the published certificates.

The exact root cause is still not final. That matters. It would be wrong to pretend that a public timeline tells us every detail of an internal ceremony, every review, or every decision.

But the important shape is already visible:

a generation defect created bad keys, then a selection and verification failure published them.

Either failure by itself could have been caught. Together, they became a browser-trust incident.

The warning that should have stopped everything

The most uncomfortable part of the public account is not the original scripting mistake. It is what reportedly happened a few weeks later.

Around May 2025, certificate revocation list signatures began failing verification.

A CRL is a signed list of certificates that should no longer be trusted. For the signature to validate, the private key used to sign the CRL must match the public key in the issuing CA certificate.

If that check fails, the system is telling you something specific:

The private key signing this CRL does not match
the public key advertised in this CA certificate.

For a CA, that should be an incident. Not a ticket to close after a configuration tweak.

Public reporting says the CRL signer was reconfigured to use the weak key set, which made the signatures verify. That removed the immediate symptom. It did not answer why two different key sets existed or why the published certificate did not match the expected HSM signing key.

This is the difference between making an alarm stop and finding out why it rang.

The missed RCA, step by step

An RCA is not a paragraph that says “wrong key was configured.” A useful RCA keeps asking until it reaches a broken control, not just the person or configuration nearest the failure.

Here is what a shallow analysis might look like:

Stage Shallow answer
Symptom CRL signatures do not verify
Immediate cause The signer is using the wrong key
Fix Point the signer at the other key
Status Closed

That is not enough, because it accepts the existence of the extra key as normal.

Here is the harder, more useful line of questioning:

Question What the investigation should establish
Why did the CRL signature fail? The signer private key did not match the public key in the intermediate certificate.
Why did they not match? The certificate request used a different key pair than the intended HSM signing key.
Why were there two key pairs? The ceremony produced extra key material during the wrap-and-unwrap test.
Why did the wrong one get selected? Labels and selection controls did not make the intended key unambiguous.
Why did nobody catch the mismatch before issuance? There was no independent post-ceremony reconciliation proving that each certificate request matched the intended HSM key.

At the second question, the incident was already discoverable.

Someone could have compared the public-key fingerprint in the certificate request with the public-key fingerprint of the HSM object. They could have inspected the key properties. They could have run a basic sanity test against the EC public point.

Any of those checks could have converted a future ecosystem-wide incident into a re-ceremony while the keys were still internal.

Why two audits did not catch it

It is tempting to hear “two audit cycles” and conclude that audits are useless. That is not the lesson.

Audits are usually designed to verify that documented controls exist and are being followed. They may witness a ceremony, sample records, review approvals, and inspect procedures. They do not necessarily recompute the security properties of every generated cryptographic key.

That gap matters here.

A ceremony can have the right people in the room, the right forms, the right HSM, and the right signatures on a checklist while still publishing a catastrophically weak key. Process evidence is not the same as cryptographic validation.

For a CA, the validation needs to include the key material itself:

  • Does the certificate request public key match the intended HSM key by fingerprint?
  • Is there exactly one approved key pair per intended intermediate?
  • Does the EC public key pass a small-scalar sanity check?
  • Do all generated key objects reconcile to the ceremony plan?
  • Has an independent tool verified the output rather than the ceremony script verifying its own work?

These are inexpensive checks compared with the cost of removing a root from browser stores.

Why revocation was not enough

eMudhra revoked the affected intermediates. That was necessary. It was not sufficient.

Revocation works only when clients fetch revocation information and decide to enforce it. Some clients do this consistently. Some soft-fail during network errors. Some do not check at all.

Browsers have additional mechanisms. Chrome and Firefox can push emergency distrust information much faster than waiting for every client to download and honour a CRL. That explains how the affected intermediates were blocked quickly after the report.

But a CA key that was publicly trusted through multiple paths needs a response that reaches more than browsers.

The affected intermediates also had cross-signed copies under Sectigo’s AAA Certificate Services. Cross-signing exists for a reasonable compatibility goal: older devices may trust the cross-signing root even when they do not have a newer eMudhra root.

In this case, compatibility became a risk multiplier.

Same weak intermediate key
        ↙                    ↘
eMudhra trust path      Sectigo cross-signed path

Blocking only the eMudhra path would not necessarily stop a client from accepting a chain through the other path. That is why browsers also had to address the cross-signed route.

Browsers were not the only thing to think about

Browser blocks are visible and fast. Backend clients are quieter.

Command-line tools, internal services, custom mobile applications, embedded devices, Java runtimes, private trust stores, and applications with pinned or stale CA bundles may not receive the same emergency protection on the same timeline.

They can also behave differently around Certificate Transparency and revocation checks.

The practical lesson for engineering teams is simple:

Do not disable certificate validation because a trust-chain migration caused a connection failure.

That turns a compatibility problem into a security bypass.

If a service breaks because a CA chain is no longer trusted, update the service’s certificates, trust store, client library, or configuration correctly. A temporary “verify false” setting is the kind of workaround that creates the next incident.

What a CA should change after this

The interesting controls here are not exotic.

1. Reconcile the ceremony output

After any key ceremony, list every HSM key object and compare it to the approved plan. There should be exactly one expected key pair per CA identity. Extra or unexpected key objects should stop the process.

2. Select keys by fingerprint, not a friendly label

Names can be similar. Operators can misread them. A SHA-256 fingerprint tied to the ceremony record is much harder to confuse.

3. Verify public keys independently

Use a separate tool and a separate reviewer to confirm that the certificate request’s public key matches the approved HSM object. The same ceremony script should not be the only thing vouching for its own result.

4. Test key quality before signing

For EC keys, check for obvious small-scalar values. For RSA keys, perform the appropriate checks for weak or shared factors. The CA should test its own signing keys at least as carefully as it tests customer certificate requests.

5. Treat unexplained crypto failures as incidents

A signature verification failure involving a CA key needs documented root cause, preserved evidence, and independent review before closure. “It works after we changed the key” is the start of an investigation, not the end.

6. Review ceremony deviations as security changes

A wrap-and-unwrap test sounds narrow. It touches secret-key handling, which makes it a security-critical change. It should have separate review, a dry run on a non-production HSM, and an output check that is independent of the changed script.

7. Re-check cross-signed intermediates

Cross-signing changes who can trust a key. Every new trust path should trigger the same key-quality verification and an explicit answer to the question: “How do we block this key everywhere if something goes wrong?”

What this means for everyone else

Most teams are not CA operators. The useful lessons still transfer.

Security checks are signals, not annoyances

If an integrity check fails, do not make it pass by changing the validation path until you understand the mismatch. The most expensive incidents often start as a warning that somebody classified as annoying.

Your automation needs an independent check

Automation is good at repeating a bad decision very quickly. When it creates credentials, certificates, signing keys, backups, or access controls, validate the output with a separate tool or control plane.

Know your trust dependencies

Every outbound HTTPS client depends on certificate validation. Inventory which applications use custom trust stores, pinned certificates, old Java bundles, embedded firmware, or unusual proxy settings before an emergency forces the question.

Rotation speed is a security control

Fast key and certificate rotation is not just convenient. It determines whether a trust incident lasts hours, days, or months.

What is still unknown

There are important open questions, and it is worth keeping them open until primary evidence answers them:

  • eMudhra’s final root-cause analysis and independent expert review
  • the exact ceremony-code defect and the controls that allowed it through
  • the complete internal handling of the May 2025 CRL signature failures
  • whether any client populations outside browser protections accepted chains from the affected keys
  • the final scope of browser and operating-system trust-store actions

Public reporting currently says there is no known exploitation before disclosure, and Chrome reported no logged TLS certificates from the six affected TLS intermediates before its block. Those facts reduce the known impact. They do not reduce the urgency of learning from the control failure.

The real headline

The headline is not that elliptic-curve cryptography failed.

It is that a security system relied on several layers of trust, yet none of those layers asked the simplest possible question soon enough:

“Does the public key we published actually belong to the secure private key we meant to use?”

For a CA, that question should be impossible to skip.

For everyone else, this is a reminder that strong cryptography only starts with the algorithm. It survives or fails based on generation, labelling, verification, review, monitoring, and how seriously teams take the first warning.

Sources

  • eMudhra certificate security incident statement
  • Cisco Talos: Compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates
  • Encryption Consulting: When the CA Key Was 4
  • Mozilla Bugzilla incident 2083449

articles.title: Your Website Changed. Did the AI Get the Memo?
articles.description: The gap between publishing a correction and seeing it reflected in an AI-generated answer is becoming...
articles.body_html:
The gap between publishing a correction and seeing it reflected in an AI-generated answer is becoming a problem that traditional SEO metrics cannot fully explain.

A website owner updates an important page. The new version fixes a technical error, clarifies a product limitation, or replaces a recommendation that is no longer safe. The content management system confirms the update. The page loads correctly in a browser. From the publisher's perspective, the information is current.

But what does the rest of the internet know?

That question has always mattered for search engine optimization (SEO). A published page still needs to be discovered, crawled, processed, indexed, and served before a search user is likely to encounter the new information. With generative engine optimization (GEO) and answer engine optimization (AEO), the question gets harder. An AI system might retrieve the current page, consult an older search index, select a different source, or answer without retrieving the page at all. Each route can produce a different account of what the publisher currently says.

Publishing is not discovery. Discovery is not indexing. Indexing is not selection. And selection is not proof that the answer reflects the current source.

Google's clocks were already complicated

At Search Central Live Deep Dive Europe in Barcelona on October 2, 2026, Google's Gary Illyes put up three slides listing typical and slowest times for 23 processes across crawling, indexing, and serving. A few of the typical figures:

  • Discovering a new URL: about 20 hours
  • Refreshing a URL Google already knows: about 30 days
  • Indexing end to end, once a page has been crawled: about 1.5 hours
  • Updating a title or snippet in results: 1 to 2 days
  • Settling a site move: 1 to 3 months

The slowest-case column is less comforting. Several rows, including discovery, refresh, and indexing, end in "never."

These numbers need context. They come from photos of the slides and attendee recaps, not from published Google documentation, and Illyes later described the slides as an exercise to see whether the audience could relate to numbers pulled internally. Nobody outside Google knows the sample size or what "typical" means. They are reference points, not service levels.

Even so, one detail in them matters a great deal for anyone publishing corrections. A new page is found faster than an old page is re-read. If you publish something new, the typical wait is measured in hours. If you fix something that already exists, the typical wait for Google to notice is measured in weeks. Corrections live on the slower clock.

Illyes also stressed that the processes are linked: a page cannot be indexed before it is crawled, so delays stack. A fast indexing pipeline cannot process a change the crawler has not seen. This is why checking a page's last crawl date in Google Search Console tells you more than repeatedly searching for the revised headline. It separates a discovery problem from a processing or presentation problem, and it gives you one observable event in the chain.

SEO, GEO, and AEO do not share one clock

SEO is largely concerned with making content discoverable, understandable, and useful within search systems. GEO and AEO extend the publisher's concern to systems that compose answers, summarize information, and cite supporting sources. The terms overlap in practice, and there is no universal technical pipeline called "GEO" that every AI product implements.

That distinction matters. Some AI answer products rely on conventional search indexes for retrieval. Some fetch pages closer to the time of the question. Some blend retrieved material with information represented in model parameters. Their source selection, caching, citation, and refresh behavior differ, and most of it is invisible to publishers.

Consider a software company that changes its documentation to say a feature requires an additional security control. A traditional search result might keep displaying an older snippet until the page is recrawled. One AI answer engine might retrieve an older indexed copy and confidently describe the previous requirement. Another might fetch the current documentation and get it right. A third might answer from an older understanding without citing the documentation at all.

None of those outcomes means the company's documentation is wrong. They show that the authority of a source and the freshness of a system's representation of that source are separate properties.

One change, one morning

I had a convenient test case. On October 23, 2026, I merged a pull request to the Sovereign Systems Specification
that added a new term page, Coverage Assertion,
and updated three existing pages to reference it. Contributor Nicolás Moreno proposed the term in the spec's GitHub
issues earlier this year, and the page gives it a specific definition: an evidence artifact asserting that a boundary
was authoritative and complete for a class of events over an interval. A term that recent and that specific makes a useful
test case. An accurate, cited answer suggests that the system has access to a current representation of the source,
although it doesn't establish precisely when or how that representation was obtained.

On the morning of October 26, three days after the merge, I checked.

Google Search Console reported the term page as not indexed. Bing Webmaster Tools reported the same. Those are useful
observations, but they describe the indexing status exposed by each tool, not everything Google's or Bing's
infrastructure might know about the page. At the time of the check, neither tool reported the page as indexed for
conventional search.

Then I asked ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini two questions, each while signed out so no personalization could help: "What is Coverage Assertion?" and the same question with "in the Sovereign Systems Specification" added.

With the source named, all three found it and cited the term page directly. ChatGPT and Perplexity both described details that exist only there, including the spec's three verification outcomes: supported, contradicted, and undetermined. Gemini credited Nicolás by name.

Asked plainly, none of them connected the term to the spec, and the ways they missed are worth a closer look.

Gemini and Perplexity both answered with confidence that a coverage assertion is a hardware verification concept: a SystemVerilog cover property that records whether a test scenario occurred. Gemini went further, saying my term is "more commonly referred to" as assertion coverage. Reverse the two words and that is a real, established term. Neither engine failed to find an answer. Each found a different one and presented it as settled. Perplexity attached citations to its version, which made it look even more authoritative. They were accurate citations for a different idea.

Same engine, same morning, signed out. Asked plainly, Gemini rewrote the term into an existing testing concept. Asked
with the source named, it found the spec.

ChatGPT did better, and it is the more instructive case. It listed several possible meanings, from software testing to
insurance, and asked where I had encountered the term. That is the honest response to an ambiguous question. It still
did not find the spec. An engine behaving well, admitting uncertainty, could not surface a page it had not selected.

Nothing in the confident answers hinted that a more specific definition existed one question away. A wrong answer
delivered that fluently does not look stale. It looks finished.

That result says two different things.

The first is about retrieval. Given the name of the source, the answer engines produced accurate, cited descriptions of
a page that Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools did not yet report as indexed. Gemini is the interesting one:
a Google product accurately described and cited a page that Google Search Console did not yet report as indexed. The
citations point at the term page rather than the GitHub discussion where the term was first proposed, but I still do not
know how each engine reached it: a live fetch at question time, or a crawler and index separate from traditional search.
The search console was the only clock I could read, and in this case it was the slow one.

The second is about selection. Without the name of the source, the page might as well not have existed. Being retrievable
when someone points at you is not the same as being chosen when someone asks the question. A reader who already knows
where to look got the current answer. A reader who simply asked did not.

That second reader is the one corrections are for. The person who most needs to learn that a security recommendation
changed is the person who does not know the page was updated, and who will never think to ask about it by name.
Retrievable is not the same as found.

The same reasoning cuts the other way for the three updated pages. Unlike the newly published term page, those pages
already existed and were subject to recrawl delays. Google's reported typical refresh interval of about 30 days provides
a useful reference point, but it is not a schedule that every page follows. An answer engine relying on an older indexed
copy could therefore be behind the origin rather than ahead of it. The lesson is not that AI is faster or slower than
search. It is that they run on different clocks, and the clock a publisher can see may not be the clock the reader's
answer came from.

This is a snapshot, not a study: one site, one change, three products, one morning. It is still enough to retire two
comfortable assumptions: that "not yet indexed" means "not yet visible," and that "retrievable" means "found."

The stale-authority problem

A link to an authoritative source is useful, but it is not evidence that the linked source was consulted in its current
form. A page can change after retrieval. A search index can lag behind the origin. A generated answer can cite the right
URL while paraphrasing an older version or drawing on another source altogether.

For readers, the distinction is easy to miss. The answer has a citation, the citation points to an official website, and
the presentation implies the claim has been checked. Yet the visible citation rarely discloses a source revision, a
retrieval timestamp, or the exact passages used. Without those details, a reader cannot tell "the system used the current
documentation" from "the system cited the documentation's URL."

Citations still make answers far easier to investigate. But a citation is a starting point for verification, not a
record of it.

This matters most for content that changed because an earlier claim was wrong. A stale product description is inconvenient.
A stale security recommendation, compliance interpretation, or medical instruction can do real harm. In those settings,
"the page is now fixed" is an incomplete account of whether the correction has reached anyone.

What can a publisher actually measure?

The first task is to stop treating "AI visibility" as a single number. A publisher can observe several different events,
each answering a different question.

Event What it tells you What it does not prove
Publication or deployment The new version exists at the origin A crawler or answer system has seen it
Search crawler visit A crawler requested the resource The changed content was indexed or used
Search indexing and presentation A search system can expose some representation of the page Every answer engine has incorporated it
AI answer mentions the topic The system can discuss the subject It used the current source
AI answer cites the page The URL was selected for attribution The answer reflects the latest revision
AI answer accurately reflects a distinctive change The output is consistent with the updated source Which retrieval path or internal evidence produced it

My morning check touched four of those rows and still could not explain the result. It also showed that the answer rows
depend heavily on how the question is asked: the same engine can pass with a pointed question and miss with a plain one.
That is normal. Search Console provides crawl and indexing signals for Google Search. Server logs, where a host provides
them, show requests from identifiable crawlers and fetchers, though a user-agent string says nothing about how the content
was used. (The spec runs on GitHub Pages, which provides none, a position many publishers share.) Controlled queries reveal
what an AI product says at a particular moment, and results vary by model, phrasing, user context, location, and time.

That is a less satisfying dashboard than one big "GEO score." It is also a more defensible one.

Structured data helps describe the source, not guarantee the answer

There is still plenty of practical work for publishers. Maintain clear internal links and a useful sitemap. Keep canonical
URLs consistent. Make important content accessible without brittle client-side interactions. Use descriptive headings and
unambiguous terminology. Where appropriate, include structured data that accurately identifies the page, its subject,
its author, and its relationships.

JSON-LD and schema.org vocabulary make those relationships easier for machines to interpret. They do not compel Google
to index a page, guarantee a rich result, or require an AI answer system to retrieve or cite the content. Treating
structured data as a promise of AI visibility swaps one measurement problem for another.

For frequently revised technical material, make changes easy to identify. Keep meaningful changelogs, stable links to
definitions, revision dates that reflect substantive updates, and, where practical, versioned documentation. These
practices let people and systems inspect a claim's history even when nobody can force faster retrieval.

Publication evidence is not consumption evidence

The same uncertainty applies to an updated API reference, a revised pricing page, or a corrected security recommendation.
That is why publication evidence and consumption evidence should not be conflated. A commit history establishes that
a change was made. A crawl date establishes that a request occurred. An answer consistent with the change establishes
what one system said, to one phrasing of one question, under particular conditions. None of those records, alone, proves
the change reached every downstream consumer.

This is not a reason to hold a correction until the ecosystem catches up. It is a reason to be precise about what
changed, make the authoritative version easy to find, and avoid claiming propagation you have not observed.

The missing receipt

In software systems, we increasingly ask for provenance: what was changed, by whom, under which authority, and with what
evidence? We should ask related questions of AI-mediated information. Which source was retrieved? When? Which version was
available? What passages supported the claim? Where did the system rely on inference rather than retrieved evidence?

Most answer engines cannot provide that level of detail today, and a publisher cannot reconstruct internal behavior it
was never allowed to observe. My commit log is a receipt for publication. Nothing yet gives me a receipt for consumption.
The honest move is to keep those separate, and to avoid turning a citation or a single good answer into a claim of
comprehensive freshness.

This is the connection between the familiar SEO delay and the emerging GEO/AEO problem. SEO gave publishers imperfect
but useful instruments for watching content move through discovery and indexing. AI answer systems add stages, and
shortcuts, where source selection and synthesis can hide which version of reality made it into the response.

The next time you update a critical page, ask more than whether the deployment succeeded or whether Google has recrawled
it. Ask what evidence would show that the correction reached the systems now answering questions on your behalf,
including for the readers who will never think to ask about your page by name.

Your website changed. Did the AI get the memo?

Sources and editorial notes

  • Barry Schwartz, Google Search Data On Crawling, Indexing & Serving Timelines, Search Engine Roundtable, Oct 5, 2026 (full tables for all 23 processes, photos of the three slides, and Illyes's "exercise" comment): https://www.seroundtable.com/google-crawling-indexing-serving-data-42225.html
  • Matt G. Southern, Google Shows How Long Crawling, Indexing & Recovery Can Take, Search Engine Journal, Oct 4, 2026 (notes the slides are not on Google's events page; no sample size or definition of "typical"): https://www.searchenginejournal.com/google-crawling-indexing-recovery-timing-ranges/591829/
  • John Campbell (ROAST), original attendee recap of day 3: https://weareroast.com/news/google-search-central-live-deep-dive-barcelona-day-3-recap/
  • Google Search Central, Ask Google to recrawl your URLs: https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/ask-google-to-recrawl
  • Google Search Central, How Search works: https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/how-search-works
  • Google Search Central, Introduction to structured data markup in Google Search: https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/structured-data/intro-structured-data
