articles.body_html:
On October 18, right in the middle of shipping a multi-feature audit and a supplement tracker redesign on my personal life_os_app (my daily Flutter Web + Cloud Firestore operating board), GitHub Actions stopped scheduling jobs. The billing meter for my personal account's hosted runner minutes had hit 100%.

Look at what my .github/workflows/ci.yml and deploy-live.yml were doing on every push and pull request:

  1. Spinning up an ubuntu-latest VM.
  2. Pulling the Flutter SDK and warming the Pub cache (~90s).
  3. Installing Python 3 and running 68 CLI sync unit tests (~15s).
  4. Running flutter analyze and 466 widget and accessibility tests (~110s).
  5. Compiling flutter build web --release --no-web-resources-cdn (~140s).
  6. Authenticating via Workload Identity Federation (google-github-actions/auth@v2) and deploying to Firebase Hosting target board (~35s).

That is 6.5 minutes per PR push and another 4 minutes on merge to main. Across 70+ PRs in October, a single-developer personal project burned through thousands of CI minutes doing work my local Apple Silicon MacBook finishes in under 35 seconds.

When your CI budget hits zero on a personal repo, you have two choices: pay for extra runner minutes to compile code your laptop already compiled, or build a deterministic local verification and deployment pipeline that is faster and safer than the YAML workflow it replaces.

Here is the exact architecture I use to keep life_os_app shipping to Firebase Hosting and Cloud Firestore with zero GitHub Actions spend.

Architecture: The Three-Layer Local Verification Gate

Moving deploys to your local machine only works if you never deploy unverified state. In life_os_app, the application state is split across two runtimes:

  • Python 3.14 CLI Sync Tools (tool/board_*.py): Morning and evening scripts that pull from Apple Reminders, Google Calendar, Harvest, Notion, and GCP Billing, then write structured JSON documents into Cloud Firestore over REST.
  • Flutter Web Client (lib/): A Riverpod 3 + Material 3 multi-skin web app served from Firebase Hosting with a custom offline Service Worker (web/offline-sw.js).

Layer 1: Firestore Schema Validation Before Every REST Write

One of the biggest risks of running CLI sync tools outside a container is accidentally clobbering fields that the Flutter Web client writes directly from the browser. For example, on the Events and Admin tabs, I tick tasks directly in the UI (config/events.taskTicks and config/admin.done), while tool/board_events.py and tool/board_admin.py sync metadata from Notion and GCP Billing.

To prevent a CLI run from wiping browser taps, tool/board_firestore.py enforces two rules before any HTTP PATCH leaves the machine:

  1. Explicit schema validation on every collection (dayPlans, stats, config, finance, plan).
  2. Field-level update masks (?updateMask.fieldPaths=...) plus hard blocks against overwriting client-owned map keys: 
# tool/board_firestore.py
if path == "config/events" and "taskTicks" in data and not fields:
    raise SystemExit(
        "refusing to overwrite config/events.taskTicks without --fields; "
        "pass --fields updated,source,events"
    )
if path == "config/admin" and "done" in data and not fields:
    raise SystemExit(
        "refusing to overwrite config/admin.done without --fields"
    )

In addition, caching the gcloud auth print-access-token call with @functools.lru_cache(maxsize=1) and enforcing a 15-second socket timeout cut multi-document Firestore sync latency by 80% and eliminated hanging background processes when switching Wi-Fi networks.

Layer 2: Per-Document Decode Isolation in Flutter Streams

In Cloud Firestore, a single malformed field inside one historical document in a collection query (collection('dayPlans').snapshots()) will normally throw a FormatException or TypeError inside .map(), killing the entire StreamProvider and replacing your UI with an error state.

During my audit pass, I hardened every repository to isolate decoding per document:

// lib/features/day_board/data/board_repository.dart
List<T> _decodeEach<T>(
  QuerySnapshot<JsonMap> query,
  T Function(JsonMap data, String id) decode,
) {
  final results = <T>[];
  for (final doc in query.docs) {
    try {
      results.add(decode(doc.data(), doc.id));
    } on Object catch (error, stackTrace) {
      developer.log(
        'Skipping malformed document ${doc.reference.path}',
        name: 'day_board.repository',
        error: error,
        stackTrace: stackTrace,
      );
    }
  }
  return results;
}

When saving multi-day edits (such as editing 7 days of focus blocks and habit notes in the This Week sheet), replacing 14 sequential await set() calls with a single atomic WriteBatch (saveWeekEditsBatch) eliminated partial-save race conditions on flaky mobile connections.

Layer 3: Self-Contained Web Bundles (--no-web-resources-cdn) & Service Worker Cleanup

When deploying Flutter Web to Firebase Hosting for daily use on iPhone, iPad, and desktop, CDN font/CanvasKit fetches can stall on airplane or train Wi-Fi. Building with --no-web-resources-cdn bundles CanvasKit and font assets directly into build/web/, paired with a custom web/offline-sw.js that races network against a 3.5-second timeout before falling back to cache:

// web/offline-sw.js
function networkFirst(request, timeoutMs) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const timer = setTimeout(() => reject(new Error('timeout')), timeoutMs);
    fetch(request)
      .then((response) => {
        if (response && response.ok) {
          caches.open(CACHE).then((cache) => cache.put(request, response.clone()));
        }
        resolve(response);
      })
      .catch(reject)
      .finally(() => clearTimeout(timer));
  }).catch(() => caches.match(request));
}

Notice the .finally(() => clearTimeout(timer)) cleanup: without it, every fast network response leaves an orphan timer running until timeoutMs expires.

Benchmarking: Cloud CI vs. Local Verification Gate

Stage GitHub Actions (ubuntu-latest) Local Apple Silicon Gate Improvement
Python CLI Unit Tests (68 tests) 14.2s (with setup) 0.02s 710x faster
Dart Format + Analyze + 466 Flutter tests 118.0s 14.5s 8.1x faster
flutter build web --release --no-web-resources-cdn 142.0s 14.8s 9.6x faster
firebase deploy --only hosting:board 34.0s 3.1s 11.0x faster
Total Wall-Clock Time ~5m 08s (plus SDK cache) ~32.4s ~9.5x faster, $0 CI cost

Table totals exclude the Flutter SDK download and Pub cache warm-up (~90s), which is what brings a full PR run to ~6.5 minutes.

Key Takeaways for Flutter & Firebase Engineers

  1. Keep CI YAML for PRs when budget allows, but make your local gate identical. A single local command (dart format -l 120 lib/ test/ && flutter analyze && python3 -m unittest discover -s tool -p '*_test.py' && flutter test) guarantees parity before firebase deploy.
  2. Use Firebase Hosting multi-site targets (hosting:board, hosting:board-staging). Mapping targets in .firebaserc lets you preview on staging or promote to live with --only hosting:board without touching sibling sites on the same GCP project.
  3. Never let one bad Firestore document take down a collection stream. Wrap per-document .fromJson() calls inside a helper that logs to dart:developer and skips the corrupted record.
  4. Test accessibility contrast and 44pt tap targets in flutter test, not in production. Running textContrastGuideline and androidTapTargetGuideline with GoogleFonts.config.allowRuntimeFetching = false catches neon text shadow contrast drops and 32pt icons in milliseconds.

The complete local release gate in one command:

dart format -l 120 lib/ test/ && \
  flutter analyze && \
  python3 -m unittest discover -s tool -p '*_test.py' && \
  flutter test && \
  flutter build web --release --no-web-resources-cdn && \
  firebase deploy --only hosting:board --project esra-life-os

articles.title: Email Bounce Types Explained: Practice Sorting Hard, Soft and Blocked Bounces in Your Browser
articles.description: 550 5.7.1 Message rejected due to content restrictions  Hard bounce? The 5 says permanent, so a...
articles.body_html:
550 5.7.1 Message rejected due to content restrictions

Hard bounce? The 5 says permanent, so a bounce handler built on "5xx means dead" files it with the dead addresses and suppresses the recipient forever. But the code is not about the address. It says a content filter at their end objected to your message, maybe over a link shortener, and the same template will likely hit that filter for other readers behind it. The usual rule, "5xx is hard, 4xx is soft", is a hint, not a verdict. This post covers the rest: where a bounce comes from in the SMTP conversation, how to read one, and which ones to suppress. Disclosure: I help build the two simulators below; they are free, run in the browser, and need no signup.

Where a bounce comes from

Most bounces start as a negative SMTP reply. If the receiving server says no during the session, your relay turns that into a bounce for you. If it accepts the message and delivery fails later, RFC 5321 says it must send a notification of its own, from the null sender <>, to your envelope MAIL FROM address. The rest come from your own relay with no reply at all: a domain that does not exist, a connection that never opens, a queue that expires. The SMTP Flow Simulator plays an illustrative timeline of the conversation in three scenarios, mixing SMTP commands with the DNS and delivery steps around them. The actors (App, SMTP relay, DNS auth, Recipient MX, Mailbox) light up in turn, and a trace pane prints each step as a C: and S: pair:

  • Successful transactional email: nine steps, from a password reset submitted on port 587 through EHLO, STARTTLS, a second EHLO, AUTH, MAIL FROM and RCPT TO, DATA, the SPF, DKIM and DMARC checks, and the relay to the recipient's MX, to inbox placement. (The simulator shows the auth checks as one step before the hand-off. In real delivery, your side signs DKIM and the receiving server runs the checks as the message arrives.)
  • Temporary greylisting retry: the recipient's MX answers RCPT TO with 451 4.7.1 Try again later, the relay backs off ("retry in 10 minutes, then 30, then 2 hours"), and the second attempt is accepted.
  • Authentication failure: 535 5.7.8 Authentication credentials invalid at AUTH, then 530 5.7.0 Authentication required when the app tries MAIL FROM anyway. Both codes come from RFC 4954. That is a rejection, not a bounce: the message never left.

Step through them with Play or Step and read the protocol notes, especially "A 250 after DATA means the next server accepted responsibility" and "Accepted does not always mean inboxed".

You can watch the start of a real conversation yourself. Receiving servers listen on port 25, and dig +short MX gmail.com gives gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com as the most preferred host (preference 5). Many home ISPs and cloud providers block outbound port 25, so this can time out. From my connection it worked, and this is the real output, with my IP swapped for a documentation address:

$ python3 -c '
import smtplib
s = smtplib.SMTP("gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com", 25, timeout=10)
print(s.ehlo("test.invalid")[1].decode())
s.quit()'
mx.google.com at your service, [203.0.113.10]
SIZE 157286400
8BITMIME
STARTTLS
ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES
PIPELINING
CHUNKING
SMTPUTF8

The line to notice is ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES. The server announces that its replies carry a second, more precise code, and that code is where bounce triage starts.

How to read a bounce

Take 550 5.1.1 User unknown. It has three parts:

  1. The reply code, 550, defined in RFC 5321. The first digit says 4 (try again later) or 5 (do not repeat this as-is).
  2. The enhanced status code, 5.1.1, defined in RFC 3463 as class.subject.detail. The middle number says what the problem is about: 1 addressing, 2 mailbox, 3 mail system, 4 network and routing, 5 protocol, 6 content, 7 security or policy.
  3. The text, free-form and often the most useful part.

The class says how long. The subject says what kind of problem it is. A few lines of Python give you a first look:

import re

SUBJECT = {"0": "other", "1": "addressing", "2": "mailbox", "3": "mail system",
           "4": "routing", "5": "protocol", "6": "content", "7": "policy"}

def first_look(reply):
    m = re.search(r"\b([45])\.(\d{1,3})\.(\d{1,3})\b", reply)
    if not m:
        return "no enhanced code, read the text"
    cls, subject, _ = m.groups()
    when = "permanent" if cls == "5" else "temporary"
    return f"{when}, about {SUBJECT.get(subject, 'other')}"

Run against three replies:

550 5.1.1 User unknown         -> permanent, about addressing
452 4.2.2 The email account th -> temporary, about mailbox
550 5.7.1 Message rejected due -> permanent, about policy

For 5.1.1, "permanent, about addressing" means a dead address: suppress it. Other addressing codes need the detail digit, since 5.1.7 and 5.1.8 are about your sender address, not theirs. "Permanent, about policy" usually points at your side: content, authentication or sending reputation. Suppressing the recipient fixes none of those. The IANA registry lists every assigned code.

Four kinds, five actions

The Bounce Triage Simulator turns this into practice. It shows twelve bounces one at a time, each with the recipient, the provider (Gmail, Outlook, Postfix, Proofpoint and others) and the raw response. For each one you answer two questions. "What kind of failure is this?": Hard bounce, Soft bounce, Blocked, or Complaint. "What do you do with it?": Suppress permanently, Retry with backoff, Fix the message then retry, Slow down then retry, or Stop sending and fix the cause. The last one is the answer for a relay denial and a blocklist listing. Press "Triage it" to see what the code means, plus a box titled "What getting it wrong costs you".

Get the kind right but the action wrong and it tells you "Right diagnosis, wrong treatment", the exact mistake it is built to catch. The rounds that teach the most:

  • 550-5.7.26 Unauthenticated email from yourdomain.com is not accepted due to domain's DMARC policy. A 5xx that is an authentication bug on your side. RFC 7372 named 5.7.26 "Multiple authentication checks failed", and Gmail uses it for DMARC failures. Receivers that enforce your DMARC policy keep rejecting mail that fails this way until you fix SPF or DKIM alignment.
  • 421 4.7.0 Too many messages from your IP. Please try again later. A 421 also closes the connection. The right action is to slow down. Retrying at the same rate makes it worse.
  • 450 4.7.1 ... Greylisted, try again in 300 seconds. Treat it as a failure and you never reach a whole class of small self-hosted domains, because the retry is the test.
  • A Yahoo feedback loop report with Feedback-Type: abuse. Not a bounce at all: the mail was delivered and the reader pressed "report spam".

Complaints get the hardest line. Suppress them at once and for good. Google's sender guidelines require every sender to keep the spam rate in Postmaster Tools below 0.3%, and recommend staying under 0.1%.

What to suppress

Seven of the twelve rounds are 5xx, and four of those seven should not be suppressed. The policy:

  • Suppress permanently: hard bounces (5.1.1 user unknown, 5.1.2 domain not found, 5.2.1 disabled mailbox) and every complaint.
  • Retry with backoff: soft bounces (4.2.2 over quota, greylisting, 4.3.0 server errors), within your relay's queue lifetime. RFC 5321 says the give-up time generally needs to be at least 4 to 5 days. It also says the retry interval SHOULD generally be at least 30 minutes, with smarter schedules when the sender knows why delivery failed, so the SMTP Flow Simulator's first greylisting retry after 10 minutes is within the rules. One expired message does not prove the address is dead.
  • Keep the recipient, investigate: 5.7.x content and authentication blocks, blocklist listings, rate limits and relay errors. Most are fixed on your side (template, DNS, send rate, delisting), some need the recipient's mail admin, and none is fixed by resending the same message unchanged.

The first digit tells you how long. The middle digit tells you what kind of problem it is. Play the three SMTP scenarios to see where replies come from, then triage the twelve bounces and count how many 5xx codes you would have suppressed by mistake. To type the conversation by hand, one command at a time, read Send an Email by Hand: The Raw SMTP Conversation.

Which bounce code has fooled your bounce handling? Tell us in the comments.

articles.title: TypeScript `ReadonlyDeep<T>` Without a Library: Writing the Recursive Utility Type Once and Never Again
articles.description: Build a production-ready ReadonlyDeep utility type that makes nested object properties immutable at compile time without external dependencies.
articles.body_html:
TypeScript ReadonlyDeep<T> Without a Library: Writing the Recursive Utility Type Once and Never Again

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Why Built-In Readonly Isn't Enough

TypeScript's built-in Readonly<T> type applies immutability to top-level properties but stops there. Nested objects remain mutable. When a developer marks a configuration object as readonly and a teammate mutates a nested property three levels deep, the compiler stays silent. The bug appears in production.

Problem flow showing built-in Readonly allowing nested mutations

A recursive readonly type solves this. Every property at every depth becomes immutable. The compiler catches mutations before they ship.

Solution flow showing ReadonlyDeep preventing all mutations

Key Takeaways

  • TypeScript's Readonly<T> only protects top-level properties; nested objects remain mutable and cause silent bugs.
  • A recursive ReadonlyDeep<T> utility type applies immutability to all properties at every depth without runtime overhead.
  • The implementation requires handling primitives, functions, arrays, Maps, Sets, and circular references with conditional types.
  • Type-fest's version adds complexity for edge cases; a focused implementation works for most codebases in under 30 lines.
  • Compiler performance degrades past 10 nesting levels or 100+ properties; measure before applying to massive schemas.

Understanding the ReadonlyDeep Signature

The type signature needs to handle every TypeScript construct. Primitives like string, number, and boolean pass through unchanged. Functions preserve their signatures. Arrays become readonly arrays. Objects recurse into their properties.

Type hierarchy showing ReadonlyDeep branching by input type

The recursive case is where the type earns its place. For each property K in object T, the type constructs a new object with K mapped to ReadonlyDeep<T[K]>. The recursion stops when it hits a primitive or function.

TypeScript's conditional types make this possible. The pattern T extends Primitive ? T : ... lets the type branch based on structure. Each branch handles a different category.

The built-in Readonly<T> handles the shallow case. ReadonlyDeep<T> wraps it with recursion. The combination creates a type that descends through arbitrarily nested structures.

Building ReadonlyDeep: The Base Case and Recursive Logic

The implementation starts with a type alias for primitives. This includes string, number, boolean, symbol, bigint, undefined, and null. Functions count as primitives here because their internal structure does not require recursion.

type Primitive =
  | string
  | number
  | boolean
  | symbol
  | bigint
  | undefined
  | null;

type ReadonlyDeep<T> = T extends Primitive
  ? T
  : T extends Function
  ? T
  : T extends (infer U)[]
  ? ReadonlyArray<ReadonlyDeep<U>>
  : {
      readonly [K in keyof T]: ReadonlyDeep<T[K]>;
    };

The first condition checks if T is a primitive. If so, the type returns T unchanged. The second condition handles functions. The third condition matches arrays using the infer pattern and wraps them in ReadonlyArray.

The final case handles objects. The mapped type iterates over every key K in T. Each property becomes readonly, and the value type becomes ReadonlyDeep<T[K]>. The recursion happens here.

This version works for most cases. A configuration object with nested arrays and objects becomes fully immutable:

interface Config {
  database: {
    host: string;
    port: number;
    credentials: {
      username: string;
      password: string;
    };
  };
  features: string[];
}

type ImmutableConfig = ReadonlyDeep<Config>;

const config: ImmutableConfig = {
  database: {
    host: "localhost",
    port: 5432,
    credentials: {
      username: "admin",
      password: "secret",
    },
  },
  features: ["caching", "logging"],
};

// All of these produce compile-time errors:
config.database.port = 3306; // Error: Cannot assign to 'port'
config.database.credentials.password = "newpass"; // Error
config.features.push("metrics"); // Error: Property 'push' does not exist
config.features[0] = "telemetry"; // Error: Index signature is readonly

The compiler blocks every mutation attempt. No runtime checks. No library dependency.

TypeScript error panel showing blocked mutations on deeply nested readonly properties

Handling Edge Cases: Functions, Maps, Sets, and Arrays

The basic implementation breaks down with Map and Set. These types have methods like set and add that mutate internal state. TypeScript's ReadonlyMap and ReadonlySet types exist for this reason.

The extended version adds conditions for these collections:

type Primitive =
  | string
  | number
  | boolean
  | symbol
  | bigint
  | undefined
  | null;

type ReadonlyDeep<T> = T extends Primitive
  ? T
  : T extends Function
  ? T
  : T extends Map<infer K, infer V>
  ? ReadonlyMap<K, ReadonlyDeep<V>>
  : T extends Set<infer U>
  ? ReadonlySet<ReadonlyDeep<U>>
  : T extends (infer U)[]
  ? ReadonlyArray<ReadonlyDeep<U>>
  : {
      readonly [K in keyof T]: ReadonlyDeep<T[K]>;
    };

The Map branch infers key and value types, wraps the value in ReadonlyDeep, and returns ReadonlyMap. The Set branch does the same with ReadonlySet. Both prevent mutations while preserving read operations.

Functions with properties require careful handling. A function can have properties attached to it, and those properties should become readonly:

interface Logger {
  (message: string): void;
  level: string;
}

type ReadonlyLogger = ReadonlyDeep<Logger>;

const logger: ReadonlyLogger = Object.assign(
  (message: string) => console.log(message),
  { level: "info" }
);

logger("test"); // Works
logger.level = "debug"; // Error: Cannot assign to 'level'

The function condition in the type needs to come after the primitive check but before the object recursion. This preserves the function signature while applying readonly to any attached properties.

Arrays of arrays require the recursion to work properly. The type string[][] becomes ReadonlyArray<ReadonlyArray<string>>. Each level of nesting applies both ReadonlyArray and ReadonlyDeep to the inner type.

For more on working with readonly collections, see ReadonlyMap and ReadonlySet in TypeScript.

ReadonlyDeep vs type-fest vs Manual Implementation

The type-fest library provides a ReadonlyDeep implementation with additional features. It handles classes, preserves function properties, and includes special cases for built-in types. The tradeoff is complexity.

Comparison of three ReadonlyDeep approaches

The custom implementation covers objects, arrays, functions, Maps, and Sets. This handles 95% of use cases in application code. Type-fest adds support for classes with private fields, WeakMaps, Promises, and other specialized types.

Here's the comparison on a complex type:

interface APISchema {
  users: Map<
    string,
    {
      profile: {
        name: string;
        tags: string[];
      };
      settings: Set<string>;
    }
  >;
  metadata: {
    version: number;
    handlers: Array<(data: unknown) => void>;
  };
}

// Custom implementation handles this correctly:
type ImmutableSchema = ReadonlyDeep<APISchema>;

// type-fest adds these guarantees:
// - Class instances preserve private field types
// - WeakMap and WeakSet get readonly versions
// - Promise values become readonly
// - Tuple types preserve length and ordering

For most codebases, the custom version works. The compiler errors guide you when edge cases appear. Adding type-fest as a dependency makes sense when you hit repeated gaps in coverage.

The maintenance burden differs. A custom utility type lives in the codebase and requires updates when TypeScript adds new built-in types. Type-fest tracks these changes and ships updates.

Teams building component libraries or TypeScript tooling benefit from type-fest's thoroughness. Application developers building features on a known stack rarely need that level of coverage.

For related patterns on partial immutability, see Partial, Required, and DeepPartial in TypeScript.

Real-World Use Cases: API Responses and Configuration Objects

API response types become safer with ReadonlyDeep. A response handler receives data from the network and should not modify it. The readonly constraint prevents accidental mutations that break caching or introduce race conditions.

interface UserResponse {
  user: {
    id: string;
    profile: {
      name: string;
      email: string;
      preferences: {
        theme: string;
        notifications: string[];
      };
    };
  };
  metadata: {
    timestamp: number;
    version: string;
  };
}

async function fetchUser(
  id: string
): Promise<ReadonlyDeep<UserResponse>> {
  const response = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`);
  return response.json();
}

async function displayUser(id: string) {
  const data = await fetchUser(id);

  // All mutation attempts blocked:
  data.user.profile.name = "Modified"; // Error
  data.user.profile.preferences.notifications.push("email"); // Error
  data.metadata.timestamp = Date.now(); // Error

  // Reading works normally:
  console.log(data.user.profile.name);
  console.log(data.user.profile.preferences.theme);
}

Data flow showing readonly API response preventing mutations

Configuration objects gain the same protection. Application config loads once at startup and should never change. Making it readonly catches bugs where code tries to modify settings based on runtime conditions.

interface AppConfig {
  server: {
    port: number;
    host: string;
    ssl: {
      enabled: boolean;
      certPath: string;
    };
  };
  database: {
    connections: Array<{
      name: string;
      url: string;
      poolSize: number;
    }>;
  };
  features: Map<string, boolean>;
}

let config: ReadonlyDeep<AppConfig>;

function loadConfig(): ReadonlyDeep<AppConfig> {
  // Load from environment or config file
  return {
    server: {
      port: 3000,
      host: "0.0.0.0",
      ssl: {
        enabled: true,
        certPath: "/etc/ssl/cert.pem",
      },
    },
    database: {
      connections: [
        {
          name: "primary",
          url: "postgresql://localhost/db",
          poolSize: 10,
        },
      ],
    },
    features: new Map([
      ["caching", true],
      ["telemetry", false],
    ]),
  };
}

function initializeApp() {
  config = loadConfig();

  // Runtime modifications blocked:
  config.server.port = 4000; // Error
  config.database.connections[0].poolSize = 20; // Error
  config.features.set("logging", true); // Error
}

IDE tooltip showing readonly error when attempting to modify nested config property

Form validation schemas work well with readonly types. The schema defines structure and constraints. Validators read from it but should not modify it. See Custom Form Validators in TypeScript for validator patterns.

State management libraries benefit from readonly types. Redux state, Zustand stores, and React context values all gain safety when typed as ReadonlyDeep. The compiler prevents direct mutations and forces proper update patterns.

Performance Considerations and Compiler Limits

TypeScript's type checker has recursion limits. Deep nesting or large object types can hit these limits and cause compilation errors. The practical limit sits around 10 levels of nesting for complex types.

Type checking performance showing degradation with nesting depth

A type with 100 properties at 3 levels deep creates 100^3 = 1,000,000 type instantiations. The compiler caches these, but initial compilation takes time. Watch for slow type checking during development.

The workaround is to limit recursion depth. Add a depth parameter that decrements with each recursion:

type Primitive =
  | string
  | number
  | boolean
  | symbol
  | bigint
  | undefined
  | null;

type ReadonlyDeep<T, Depth extends number = 10> = Depth extends 0
  ? Readonly<T>
  : T extends Primitive
  ? T
  : T extends Function
  ? T
  : T extends Map<infer K, infer V>
  ? ReadonlyMap<K, ReadonlyDeep<V, Prev<Depth>>>
  : T extends Set<infer U>
  ? ReadonlySet<ReadonlyDeep<U, Prev<Depth>>>
  : T extends (infer U)[]
  ? ReadonlyArray<ReadonlyDeep<U, Prev<Depth>>>
  : {
      readonly [K in keyof T]: ReadonlyDeep<T[K], Prev<Depth>>;
    };

type Prev<N extends number> = N extends 0
  ? 0
  : N extends 1
  ? 0
  : N extends 2
  ? 1
  : N extends 3
  ? 2
  : N extends 4
  ? 3
  : N extends 5
  ? 4
  : N extends 6
  ? 5
  : N extends 7
  ? 6
  : N extends 8
  ? 7
  : N extends 9
  ? 8
  : N extends 10
  ? 9
  : never;

This version stops recursing after 10 levels and falls back to shallow Readonly. The Prev helper decrements the depth counter. When depth reaches zero, recursion stops.

Measure compilation time with tsc --diagnostics. Look for the "Type checking time" metric. If it exceeds one second, investigate which types cause the slowness.

Large codebases should apply ReadonlyDeep selectively. Configuration objects, API responses, and constants benefit from it. Internal implementation types that change frequently create unnecessary compilation overhead.

The type system overhead is zero at runtime. ReadonlyDeep is purely a compile-time construct. The JavaScript output contains no traces of it.

Frequently Asked Questions

How does ReadonlyDeep differ from const assertions?

Const assertions make literal types as narrow as possible and add shallow readonly to objects. ReadonlyDeep applies deep immutability to existing type definitions. Use const assertions for inline objects and ReadonlyDeep for reusable types.

Can ReadonlyDeep handle circular references?

No. Circular type references cause infinite recursion in TypeScript's type checker. The depth-limited version prevents compiler hangs but does not make circular structures readonly. Avoid circular references or use shallow Readonly for those cases.

Does ReadonlyDeep work with generics?

Yes. Pass generic types to ReadonlyDeep like any other type. The recursion applies to whatever type the generic resolves to at usage time.

Will ReadonlyDeep prevent all runtime mutations?

No. TypeScript types disappear at runtime. ReadonlyDeep provides compile-time safety only. Use Object.freeze() for runtime immutability or combine both approaches for defense in depth.

Should every type use ReadonlyDeep by default?

No. Apply it to data that should not change: configuration, API responses, constants. Internal implementation types that undergo frequent mutations benefit from normal mutability. Overuse creates friction without safety gains.

Write It Once, Use It Forever

The ReadonlyDeep<T> utility type solves the nested mutability problem that built-in Readonly<T> leaves open. Thirty lines of code eliminate an entire class of bugs. The compiler catches mutations at every depth before they reach production.

The implementation handles objects, arrays, functions, Maps, and Sets. Edge cases exist but rarely matter in application code. Teams that need comprehensive coverage can reach for type-fest. Teams building features on standard types can write this once and never think about it again.

Configuration objects and API responses gain immediate safety benefits. State management becomes more predictable. The type system enforces immutability contracts that previously existed only in documentation.

Compilation time matters for large schemas. Measure performance and limit recursion depth when needed. The tradeoff between safety and build speed is concrete and measurable.

Adding this utility type to a codebase takes five minutes and prevents mutations that take hours to debug.

articles.title: Your AI said "fixed" but never ran the tests? I made a plugin that won't let it say "done" until they pass

articles.body_html:
You ask Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, etc. for a quick fix. It changes the code and says "Fixed ✅". Later you find out it never ran a single test, or ran them through | tail and missed 58 failures.

So I built proof-of-done, a free Claude Code plugin: Claude simply can't finish until the tests, build or lint have passed after its last edit.

Try it inside Claude Code (free, source on GitHub):

/plugin marketplace add WST2002/claude-code-skills
/plugin install proof-of-done@claude-code-skills

A real Claude Code session, shortened: Claude said "fixed" without testing, the plugin made it run the tests, and they found a second bug.

What happened in that session

  • I asked: "SAVE10 gives the wrong total, fix it quickly, no need to run the tests."
  • Claude edited price.js and said "Fixed."
  • proof-of-done blocked the stop: "You changed 1 code file (price.js) but ran no verification after your last edit. Run: npm run test"
  • Claude ran the tests. One failed: with the FLAT50 coupon the total became −₹20. Claude had never seen that bug.
  • It fixed that too, and all 4 tests passed. Now it was really done.

How it works

1. It watches every edit and every check

  • Hooks record each code edit and each test, build or lint run, with its exit code.
  • It finds your project's commands on its own: npm, pnpm, yarn, bun, pytest, Go, Cargo, Maven, Gradle, .NET, make.

2. When Claude tries to stop, it asks: is there proof?

  • No run after the last edit → blocked, with the exact command to run.
  • The last run failed → blocked, with the exit code.

3. It doesn't accept fake proof

  • Exit code hidden by | tail, | head or || true → blocked.
  • The run passed but 0 tests ran (all skipped, or no test files found, including Go's [no test files] and Jest's --passWithNoTests) → blocked.
  • A check that failed, then passed with no edit in between → flagged as flaky.

4. It catches test tampering

  • Tests skipped or focused (.skip, .only, @pytest.mark.skip), assertions weakened (toBe(250) → toBeDefined()), tests deleted, errors hidden (@ts-ignore, eslint-disable), coverage thresholds lowered: blocked with the file and line.

5. New code with no test? It asks you once

  • If Claude added real code but no test, it asks you whether to add one. Say no, and the report notes why. Small edits, styles and config are left alone.

Get it

  • Install: the two commands above, inside Claude Code
  • Source (MIT, runs only on your laptop, no network calls): proof-of-done on GitHub
  • All my Claude Code skills: github.com/WST2002/claude-code-skills
  • More short demos: youtube.com/@wst2002rk

articles.title: AI wrote the first 90% of my app in an afternoon. The last 10% took three weeks.
articles.description: There's an old programmer's joke: the first 90% of the code takes 90% of the time, and the remaining...
articles.body_html:
There's an old programmer's joke: the first 90% of the code takes 90% of the time, and the remaining 10% takes the other 90% of the time. I used to tell it as a joke.

Then I let AI write a whole SaaS — auth, Stripe billing, a dashboard, a public API — and the joke stopped being funny. Because AI made the first 90% genuinely instant. And the second 90% was still exactly where it had always been, waiting for me, untouched.

The demo worked in an afternoon. The product took three more weeks. This is a field report on the gap between those two things — the part no demo ever shows you.

The first 90% really is solved

Let me be fair to the machine, because the first part was astonishing.

"Set up a Next.js app with Postgres and Drizzle, auth, a billing flow, a dashboard, and a public API." It did it. Correctly. In close to one shot. The scaffolding, the CRUD, the Zod schemas, the table with sorting and pagination — the stuff I actively dislike writing — came out clean, first try, no notes. By the end of day one I had something I could click through and demo to a friend. It looked done.

That's the trap. It looked done because everything that's easy to build is also easy to show. The demo path is the happy path, and the happy path is the 90% that was never the hard part.

The rule: the speed you feel in the first afternoon is real — and it's measuring the wrong thing. "I can demo it" and "it's done" are separated by the entire job.

The last 10% isn't code. It's anticipation.

Here's what the remaining three weeks were actually made of. None of it showed up in the demo, because the demo was one well-behaved user doing exactly what I expected.

  • The empty state. Day one, the dashboard has no data. The AI rendered a table with headers and a blank void underneath — technically correct, and it makes a brand-new user think the product is broken. There's no "add your first client" nudge, because I never asked for one, because in my head the table always had data in it.
  • The error state. The checkout worked perfectly — with a card that approves. The first time a real card got declined, the button just… hung. No message, no retry, no path forward. The AI built the road and no guardrail, because I'd only ever described the road.
  • The double-click. A user on a slow connection clicked "Subscribe" twice. Two Stripe subscriptions, one customer. The happy path fires once; real humans mash buttons.
  • The race. Same record open in two tabs, both saved. Last write wins, the other silently gone. Fine in a demo where one person clicks one thing at a time.
  • The 2am weirdo. A session that expired overnight, a stale dashboard left open, one click in the morning → a 401 the UI had no idea what to do with → white screen. "Handles a user doing something weird at 2am" is a different product from "handles me, awake, clicking in order."
  • The public API with no armor. No rate limiting. No stable pagination. No idempotency key on the POST, so a retried request quietly created the thing twice. All the behaviors that aren't features — they're the absence of disasters.

Every one of these compiled. Every one passed the happy-path test. Not one of them was in the demo. This is the last 10%, and it's made almost entirely of things you only know to build because you've been burned by their absence.

The first 90% is construction. The last 10% is anticipation. AI is extraordinary at the first and has none of the second.

Why the AI can't close the gap

It's tempting to say "the model just isn't good enough yet." That's not what I found. The model built every single one of those fixes correctly the moment I described them. "Add an empty state." "Handle a declined card." "Debounce the submit." "Add an idempotency key." Done, done, done, done — perfectly.

The problem was never that it couldn't write the code. The problem is that it builds exactly what you describe, and the last 10% is precisely the stuff you don't think to describe. It has no scar tissue. It has never been woken at 2am by the empty state it forgot. So it will cheerfully hand you a demo and call it done, and it will be right that it's done — for the one user it imagined, who is always you, awake, behaving.

The rule: the AI closes the gap the instant you point at it. Knowing where to point is the whole job — and knowing where to point is just a list of every edge case that ever hurt you.

The uncomfortable part

So here's what actually happened to the shape of the work.

The first 90% — the part that felt like engineering, the typing, the construction, the thing that looks like progress on a screen share — collapsed to near zero. What's left is the part that never looked like much: sitting there cold, asking "what happens if they do this instead?" over and over until you've imagined every stupid, hostile, half-asleep thing a stranger will do to your software.

That part didn't get faster. If anything it got more exposed, because AI stripped away the busywork that used to disguise how much of the real job it always was. We told ourselves building software was mostly typing. It was mostly anticipating; the typing just took long enough to hide that.

And that's the senior skill. Not syntax. Not "knows the framework." The ability to look at a working demo and feel, in your gut, the nineteen ways it'll break in front of a real person. You don't get that from a model. You get it from having shipped the empty state that made someone think your product was broken, once, and never forgetting.

What I actually changed

I didn't stop using AI — I let it write 100% of the first 90%, and I'd never scaffold by hand again. I changed where I spend my attention, and how I define "done":

  • "Demo works" is the start of the work, not the end. The afternoon it clicks through is day one. I now budget the real schedule around the 10%, because that's the 90%.
  • I write the edge cases down before I build, not after they bite. Empty, error, loading, double-click, concurrent, expired, retried. It's a checklist now, because the model will never volunteer it and I will never remember all of it under pressure.
  • The thing that writes the code is never the thing that decides it's done. A separate reviewer, prompted to break the diff — "what does a hostile, half-asleep user do here?" — catches the missing states the author waves right past, because the author's mental model is the happy path by construction.

Author writes it, a skeptic tries to break it, a human owns the call on whether it's actually finished. That separation is the only reason I can hand the typing to a machine and still ship something that survives contact with a real user. It's also how we build Xenition — our AI workspace: describe the tool you want in plain language and it builds and deploys the working app, real database and real URL. The describing is instant now. The deciding-what-to-describe is still the job, and it always will be.

Would I do it again?

In a heartbeat. The first 90% in an afternoon is not a gimmick — it's the biggest change to how I build in a decade, and I'm never giving it back.

But I'd walk in knowing what the demo is lying about. "It works" means it works for the user you imagined. The last 10% is the work of imagining the ones you didn't — and that was always the whole job. AI just took away everything that used to hide it.

articles.title: How I finally understood the Liskov Substitution Principle
articles.description: The Intro   Halfway through SOLID! We are at the L, the one with the scary name: the Liskov...
articles.body_html:
The Intro

Halfway through SOLID! We are at the L, the one with the scary name: the Liskov Substitution Principle.

If the previous two felt like common sense with fancy labels, this one is the first that usually catches people off guard. I have shipped the exact bug we are about to write. More than once. 🙃

The What

The original definition is a math paper from 1987 and reads like one:

If S is a subtype of T, then objects of type T may be replaced with objects of type S without altering any of the desirable properties of the program.

Let me translate: if your code works with the parent, it must also work with any child, without surprises. No instanceof checks, no "oh but not that one".

The usual example is squares and rectangles. I have never once had a square in production, so let's do something you will actually run into: payments and refunds.

The How

Our store accepts a few ways to pay. Each one can charge and refund:

// src/payment-method.ts
export abstract class PaymentMethod {
  abstract charge(amount: number): Promise<void>
  abstract refund(amount: number): Promise<void>
}

// src/card-payment.ts
import { PaymentMethod } from './payment-method.js'

export class CardPayment extends PaymentMethod {
  async charge(amount: number) {
    console.log(`💳 charged $${amount}`)
  }

  async refund(amount: number) {
    console.log(`💳 refunded $${amount}`)
  }
}

// src/paypal-payment.ts
import { PaymentMethod } from './payment-method.js'

export class PaypalPayment extends PaymentMethod {
  async charge(amount: number) {
    console.log(`🅿️ charged $${amount}`)
  }

  async refund(amount: number) {
    console.log(`🅿️ refunded $${amount}`)
  }
}

And the part that uses them never cares which one it got:

// src/refund-service.ts
import type { PaymentMethod } from './payment-method.js'

interface Order {
  id: string
  total: number
  paidWith: PaymentMethod
}

export class RefundService {
  async refundAll(orders: Order[]) {
    for (const order of orders) {
      await order.paidWith.refund(order.total)
      console.log(`✅ order ${order.id} refunded`)
    }
  }
}

Beautiful. Substitutable. Barbara Liskov would be proud.

Then product adds gift cards. Gift cards can be charged, obviously. But legal says gift cards can't be refunded to cash. So we write the "obvious" thing:

// src/gift-card-payment.ts
import { PaymentMethod } from './payment-method.js'

export class GiftCardPayment extends PaymentMethod {
  async charge(amount: number) {
    console.log(`🎁 charged $${amount}`)
  }

  async refund() {
    throw new Error('Gift cards cannot be refunded')
  }
}

It compiles. TypeScript is happy. The PR gets approved. 🚢

Three weeks later a product gets recalled and support runs the "refund everyone who bought it" script:

// src/main.ts
import { RefundService } from './refund-service.js'
import { CardPayment } from './card-payment.js'
import { GiftCardPayment } from './gift-card-payment.js'

const orders = [
  { id: 'A1', total: 40, paidWith: new CardPayment() },
  { id: 'A2', total: 25, paidWith: new GiftCardPayment() },
  { id: 'A3', total: 60, paidWith: new CardPayment() },
]

await new RefundService().refundAll(orders)

Output:

💳 refunded $40
✅ order A1 refunded
Error: Gift cards cannot be refunded

Order A1 refunded. Order A2 blew up. Order A3? Never happened. Customer A3 is now writing a one-star review.

That's a Liskov violation. RefundService was written against PaymentMethod, and the contract of PaymentMethod says "I can refund". GiftCardPayment said it was a PaymentMethod and then broke the promise at runtime.

The usual "fix" makes it worse:

if (order.paidWith instanceof GiftCardPayment) continue

Now RefundService knows about gift cards. Tomorrow it has to know about store credit. Then crypto. The whole point of the base class was to not know.

Step 1: stop lying in the type

The real problem is that the parent promised something not every child can keep. So let's make the promise smaller:

// src/payment-method.ts
export interface PaymentMethod {
  charge(amount: number): Promise<void>
}

export interface Refundable {
  refund(amount: number): Promise<void>
}

(Yes, we swapped the abstract class for interfaces. There was no shared code in the base anyway.)

Step 2: each method tells the truth 

// src/card-payment.ts
import type { PaymentMethod, Refundable } from './payment-method.js'

export class CardPayment implements PaymentMethod, Refundable {
  async charge(amount: number) {
    console.log(`💳 charged $${amount}`)
  }

  async refund(amount: number) {
    console.log(`💳 refunded $${amount}`)
  }
}

// src/gift-card-payment.ts
import type { PaymentMethod } from './payment-method.js'

export class GiftCardPayment implements PaymentMethod {
  async charge(amount: number) {
    console.log(`🎁 charged $${amount}`)
  }
}

No refund() on the gift card. No throw. It just doesn't claim to be something it isn't.

Step 3: ask for exactly what you need 

// src/refund-service.ts
import type { Refundable } from './payment-method.js'

interface RefundableOrder {
  id: string
  total: number
  paidWith: Refundable
}

export class RefundService {
  async refundAll(orders: RefundableOrder[]) {
    for (const order of orders) {
      await order.paidWith.refund(order.total)
      console.log(`✅ order ${order.id} refunded`)
    }
  }
}

And now the best part. Go back to main.ts and try to pass a gift card order into refundAll():

Type 'GiftCardPayment' is not assignable to type 'Refundable'.
  Property 'refund' is missing in type 'GiftCardPayment'.

The compiler caught it. At build time. Not at 2 PM on recall day.

Whoever writes the refund script now has to decide up front what to do with gift card orders (issue store credit, email the customer, whatever). The decision moved from "a crash in a loop" to "a red squiggle in the editor".

The Why

Let's be explicit about the lesson, because it is subtle:

  • Inheritance is a promise, not a shortcut. "GiftCard is a PaymentMethod" sounded right in English. In code, it meant "GiftCard can do everything PaymentMethod can do", and that was false.
  • A method that throws NotSupported is a red flag. If a child has to disable a parent's method, the parent's contract is too big. Shrink it.
  • Callers depend on the smallest thing they need. RefundService needs refunds, so it asks for Refundable. Not PaymentMethod. Not CardPayment.
  • The type system becomes your QA. Every wrong combination fails to compile instead of failing in production.

If you remember one sentence: a subclass may do more than its parent, never less.

The Goodbye

Did you notice that fixing the L made us split one fat interface into two thin ones? That's not a coincidence. That's the I (Interface Segregation) knocking on the door, and it's up next.

Go search your codebase for throw new Error('not supported'). I'll wait. Happy coding 🤝

articles.title: The CRDT That Throws Itself Away: Inside Eg-walker
articles.description: Here's a number from a recent systems paper that stopped me cold.  Take the real editing history of...
articles.body_html:
Here's a number from a recent systems paper that stopped me cold.

Take the real editing history of Git's own Makefile, reconstructed from the Git repository, with its many authors and branches. Merge it with a classic Operational Transformation algorithm, and it takes one hour. Merge it with an algorithm called Eg-walker, and it takes 24 milliseconds.

Eg-walker comes from Joseph Gentle and Martin Kleppmann, in the paper Collaborative Text Editing with Eg-walker: Better, Faster, Smaller, presented at EuroSys 2025. What makes it interesting isn't just the speed. It's the trick behind it: a CRDT that only exists for the duration of a merge and is then thrown away.

If you've worked with collaborative editing, you know the trade-off this breaks. Let's look at how.

The trade-off everyone has lived with

There are two families of algorithms for collaborative text.

Operational Transformation (OT) stores the document as plain text and transforms concurrent operations against each other. It's memory-light and loads instantly, which is why Google Docs, Microsoft Office, and Overleaf use it. The problem is merging. If two users each made n edits while apart, every edit from one side has to be transformed against every edit from the other. That's at least O(n²), and some OT algorithms are cubic or worse. Fine for real-time typing with small n. Painful for offline work or long-running branches.

CRDTs give every character a unique ID and store positions relative to other IDs. Merging long branches is fine, and they work peer-to-peer. But that metadata has to be loaded from disk and held in memory the entire time a document is open, even when nobody else is editing. The paper measured that even the best CRDTs today use more than ten times the memory of OT just to view and edit a document.

So you pick: slow merges, or heavy documents.

Insight 1: store the history, not the state

Eg-walker starts by changing what gets stored and replicated.

Instead of CRDT metadata, every replica keeps an event graph: a DAG of every edit, where each event holds three things. An ID, the IDs of its parent events, and the operation exactly as the user performed it. That means plain index-based operations like Insert(3, "l") or Delete(1), never transformed, never rewritten.

If that sounds like Git, it should. The parents of an event record what its author had seen when they made it. Two events are concurrent if neither is an ancestor of the other, just like two commits on different branches.

This gives a clean definition of the problem. The document is simply:

document = replay(eventGraph)

where replay is a deterministic function. Any two replicas with the same set of events must produce the same document. Everything else is about making replay fast.

Insight 2: you only need a CRDT when there's concurrency

Here's the observation the whole algorithm rests on.

When you type locally, your edit's parent is the current state of the document. When a remote edit arrives that was made after everything you already have, its parent is also the current state. In both cases, there's nothing to transform. The edit's index is already correct, and you can apply it directly to a plain string.

Transformation is only needed when concurrent events meet. And in most real editing histories, concurrency is rare. Authors take turns, or there's only one author.

So Eg-walker keeps three things per replica:

  1. The event graph, on disk.
  2. The document, as plain text, in memory. No metadata at all.
  3. An internal CRDT state, which is temporary. It's built only to merge concurrent edits and then discarded. It's never saved to disk and never sent over the network.

Most of the time, the third item doesn't exist.

How replay works

When concurrent events do need merging, Eg-walker walks the event graph in topological order and builds its temporary CRDT as it goes. The clever part is that the CRDT tracks the document at two versions at once:

  • The effect version: the document with every event processed so far applied. This only moves forward.
  • The prepare version: the document exactly as the author of the current event saw it. This moves backward and forward.

Why two versions? Because an event like Delete(1) means "delete whatever was at index 1 in the author's view." To find the right character, you need the author's view (prepare). To know where that character sits in the real merged document, you need the full view (effect).

Each character gets one record in a list, including deleted ones. Each record holds two small states:

  • Prepare state: NotInsertedYet, Ins, or Del n (deleted by n concurrent deletions in the prepare view).
  • Effect state: Ins or Del.

And three operations move things around:

  • apply(e): interpret e in the prepare version, update both versions, and output the transformed operation for the real document.
  • retreat(e): make the prepare version behave as if e never happened.
  • advance(e): make e take effect in the prepare version again.

A walkthrough

Let's use the paper's own example. The document starts as hi. One user changes it to hey. At the same time, another user capitalizes it to Hi. After syncing, someone adds !.

Event Operation Branch
e1, e2 Insert h, Insert i shared start: hi
e3, e4 Insert(0, H), Delete(1) user B: Hi
e5, e6, e7 Delete(1), Insert(1, e), Insert(2, y) user A: hey
e8 Insert(3, !), parents: e4 and e7 after merging

Replaying in order:

  1. Apply e1 to e4. Each event's parent is the previous one, so nothing to adjust. The internal records are H, h (deleted), i, and the real document is Hi.
  2. Before e5, retreat e4 and e3. User A never saw B's edits, so the prepare version must forget them. H becomes NotInsertedYet, and h becomes Ins again. The effect state doesn't change: the real document is still Hi.
  3. Apply e5, e6, e7. A's Delete(1) is interpreted against A's view, hi, so it deletes i. A's inserts land after h in the record list. But when converted to the effect version, they're counted relative to the real document, which contains H. The real document becomes Hey.
  4. Before e8, advance e3 and e4. e8's author had seen both branches, so B's edits are brought back into the prepare view.
  5. Apply e8. Insert(3, "!") is interpreted against Hey, and the result is Hey!.

Notice what happened in step 3. A's Delete(1) was index-based, written against a document that never existed on B's machine. Retreating and advancing let the algorithm reconstruct exactly the view A had, at the cost of a few state flips.

A toy implementation

Here's a deliberately simple version in JavaScript, about 80 lines for the core. It skips all the performance work (more on that below), but it follows the algorithm's structure: topological sort, prepare/effect states, retreat/advance, and transformed output.

const NOT_INSERTED = -1, INS = 0; // sp: -1 not yet inserted, 0 inserted, n>0 deleted n times

export class EventGraph {
  constructor() { this.events = new Map(); }
  add(e) { this.events.set(e.id, e); return e; }

  // Lamport timestamp: one more than the max of the parents
  lamport(id) {
    const e = this.events.get(id);
    if (e._lt === undefined) e._lt = 1 + Math.max(0, ...e.parents.map(p => this.lamport(p)));
    return e._lt;
  }

  ancestors(ids) { // a version plus everything that happened before it
    const out = new Set(), stack = [...ids];
    while (stack.length) {
      const id = stack.pop();
      if (out.has(id)) continue;
      out.add(id);
      stack.push(...this.events.get(id).parents);
    }
    return out;
  }

  topoSort(shuffle = false) {
    const children = new Map(), order = [], seen = new Set();
    for (const e of this.events.values()) {
      for (const p of e.parents) {
        if (!children.has(p)) children.set(p, []);
        children.get(p).push(e.id);
      }
    }
    const visit = (id) => {
      if (seen.has(id)) return;
      if (!this.events.get(id).parents.every(p => seen.has(p))) return;
      seen.add(id); order.push(id);
      const kids = [...(children.get(id) || [])];
      if (shuffle) kids.sort(() => Math.random() - 0.5);
      for (const k of kids) visit(k);
    };
    const roots = [...this.events.values()].filter(e => e.parents.length === 0).map(e => e.id);
    if (shuffle) roots.sort(() => Math.random() - 0.5);
    for (const r of roots) visit(r);
    return order;
  }
}

export function replay(graph, { shuffle = false } = {}) {
  const order = graph.topoSort(shuffle);
  const pos = new Map(order.map((id, i) => [id, i]));
  const records = [];       // temporary CRDT: one record per character, incl. tombstones
  const target = new Map(); // event id -> record it touched
  let prepare = [];         // current prepare version
  let doc = '';             // the real document (effect version)

  const cmp = (a, b) =>     // total order on events: Lamport timestamp, then agent
    graph.lamport(a) - graph.lamport(b) ||
    (graph.events.get(a).agent < graph.events.get(b).agent ? -1 : 1);

  const nthVisibleInPrepare = (n) => {
    let seen = -1;
    for (let i = 0; i < records.length; i++)
      if (records[i].sp === INS && ++seen === n) return i;
    return -1;
  };
  const effectIndex = (recIdx) =>
    records.slice(0, recIdx).filter(r => r.se === INS).length;

  for (const id of order) {
    const e = graph.events.get(id);

    // 1. Move the prepare version to e.parents
    const oldSet = graph.ancestors(prepare), newSet = graph.ancestors(e.parents);
    const toRetreat = [...oldSet].filter(x => !newSet.has(x)).sort((a, b) => pos.get(b) - pos.get(a));
    const toAdvance = [...newSet].filter(x => !oldSet.has(x)).sort((a, b) => pos.get(a) - pos.get(b));
    for (const x of toRetreat) {
      const r = target.get(x);
      r.sp = graph.events.get(x).type === 'ins' ? NOT_INSERTED : r.sp - 1;
    }
    for (const x of toAdvance) {
      const r = target.get(x);
      r.sp = graph.events.get(x).type === 'ins' ? INS : r.sp + 1;
    }

    // 2. Apply e, interpreting its index in the prepare version
    if (e.type === 'ins') {
      let i = e.index === 0 ? 0 : nthVisibleInPrepare(e.index - 1) + 1;
      // Tie-break among concurrent inserts at the same spot (RGA-style rule)
      while (i < records.length && records[i].sp === NOT_INSERTED && cmp(records[i].id, id) > 0) i++;
      const rec = { id, ch: e.ch, sp: INS, se: INS };
      records.splice(i, 0, rec);
      target.set(id, rec);
      const at = effectIndex(i);
      doc = doc.slice(0, at) + e.ch + doc.slice(at);   // transformed op: insert at `at`
    } else {
      const i = nthVisibleInPrepare(e.index);
      const rec = records[i];
      target.set(id, rec);
      rec.sp += 1;
      if (rec.se === INS) {
        const at = effectIndex(i);
        rec.se = 'del';
        doc = doc.slice(0, at) + doc.slice(at + 1);    // transformed op: delete at `at`
      }                                                // already deleted elsewhere: no-op
    }
    prepare = [id];
  }
  return doc;
}

And a tiny helper to record edits the way a real editor would, with each event's parents set to whatever its author had seen:

export function makeAgent(graph, name) {
  let seq = 0, frontier = [];
  return {
    get frontier() { return frontier; },
    set frontier(f) { frontier = f; },
    ins(index, ch) {
      const e = graph.add({ id: `${name}${++seq}`, agent: name, type: 'ins', index, ch, parents: frontier });
      frontier = [e.id];
    },
    del(index) {
      const e = graph.add({ id: `${name}${++seq}`, agent: name, type: 'del', index, parents: frontier });
      frontier = [e.id];
    },
  };
}

Now replay the walkthrough:

const g = new EventGraph();
const a = makeAgent(g, 'a'), b = makeAgent(g, 'b');

a.ins(0, 'h'); a.ins(1, 'i');           // shared start: "hi"
b.frontier = a.frontier;

b.ins(0, 'H'); b.del(1);                // B: "Hi"
a.del(1); a.ins(1, 'e'); a.ins(2, 'y'); // A: "hey"

a.frontier = [...b.frontier, ...a.frontier]; // A syncs with B
a.ins(3, '!');

console.log(replay(g)); // "Hey!"

Every operation in the graph is stored exactly as typed. replay produces Hey!. Run it with { shuffle: true } and you get a different traversal order but the same result.

Two honest caveats about this toy. It uses a simple RGA-style rule to order concurrent insertions at the same position, while the authors use a variant of the Yjs algorithm designed to avoid interleaving concurrent runs of text. And it replays everything from scratch with linear scans, which brings us to the part that makes the real thing fast.

Insight 3: critical versions let you forget

A critical version is a point in the history where everything before it happened before everything after it. No branch crosses it. In a linear editing session, every single version is critical.

The paper's key observation is that critical versions split the history into independent sections. Events before one can't affect how events after it are transformed. That enables two optimizations:

  • Whenever replay reaches a critical version, the entire internal state can be thrown away. It's replaced with a single placeholder record meaning "some unknown text is here."
  • If an event and its parent are both critical, it's emitted unchanged. No CRDT work at all.

So when a concurrent edit arrives later, Eg-walker doesn't replay from the beginning of time. It finds the most recent critical version before the concurrency, starts from a placeholder, replays only the events since then, and applies the new ones.

For a document that's mostly edited by one person at a time, that means almost the entire history is skipped.

What the benchmarks show

The authors tested on real editing traces: sequential writing, real-time collaboration, and histories reconstructed from Git repositories. They compared their Rust implementation against Automerge, Yjs, their own optimized reference CRDT, and an OT implementation.

  • Merging long branches: On the Git Makefile trace, OT took an hour while Eg-walker took 24 ms, about 160,000 times faster.
  • Sequential editing: Eg-walker was 7 to 10 times faster than their reference CRDT, which itself outperformed both Yjs and Automerge.
  • Memory: In the steady state, while a document is open for editing, Eg-walker used 1 to 2 orders of magnitude less memory than the best CRDT.
  • Loading: Like OT, a document loads as plain text, orders of magnitude faster than the CRDTs tested.

The trade-offs

It isn't free, and the paper is upfront about where it costs.

Peak memory during a merge is CRDT-sized. While merging, Eg-walker's peak memory is roughly comparable to a CRDT's steady state. It's only cheap between merges.

Heavily concurrent histories gain little. On traces with constant concurrency, merge time was similar to their reference CRDT, because there are few critical versions to exploit. One trace had none at all.

Traversal order matters. On highly concurrent histories, a poorly chosen topological order made merging up to 8 times slower. The real implementation uses a heuristic to avoid that.

The worst case is O(n² log n). The authors note it's unlikely in real editing histories, but it exists.

You still store history. The event graph must be kept as long as concurrent edits might still arrive. It compresses well, but it's a cost.

It's plain text, for now. The paper covers plain text only, and the authors believe the approach can extend to rich text and other formats. That's not trivial: the team behind the Loro library, which draws on Eg-walker's ideas, has written that the original Peritext rich-text algorithm couldn't be used on top of it directly.

Why it matters

For years, the practical advice was: if you want lightweight, fast-loading documents, use OT and a central server. If you want offline editing and peer-to-peer sync, use a CRDT and pay for it in memory.

Eg-walker suggests that was a false choice. Keep the immutable history, keep the document as plain text, and build the CRDT only for the moment you actually need it.

If you want to dig deeper, the authors' production Rust implementation lives in Diamond Types, and there's a TypeScript reference implementation written for readability. The paper itself is very readable too.

I'm curious whether anyone here has run into the OT vs. CRDT trade-off in production. Which side did you pick, and would something like this have changed your decision?
