articles.description: Introduction   Working with a database from code usually means one of two pains: writing raw...
articles.body_html:
Introduction

Working with a database from code usually means one of two pains: writing raw SQL strings (powerful, but no autocomplete and easy to mistype) or learning a heavy ORM with its own query language. Prisma, released in 2019, offers a third way for TypeScript and Node developers: define your data model once in a readable schema file, and Prisma generates a type-safe client — so database queries get autocomplete, type checking, and errors at write time instead of runtime.

Schema first, then a generated client

The workflow has three parts. First, a schema file describes your tables:

model User {
  id    Int    @id @default(autoincrement())
  email String @unique
  name  String
  posts Post[]
}
model Post {
  id       Int    @id @default(autoincrement())
  title    String
  authorId Int
  author   User   @relation(fields: [authorId], references: [id])
}

Second, Prisma Migrate turns schema changes into versioned migration files, so the database evolves safely alongside the code. Third, the generated client lets you query with ordinary TypeScript that the compiler checks:

const user = await prisma.user.findUnique({
  where: { email: "ayesha@example.com" },
  include: { posts: true },
});

A typo in a field name becomes a compile error, not a broken query in production — and the relation (posts) loads in the same call, without hand-writing a join (the SQL post's joins, done for you).

The honest trade

Prisma's trade is abstraction: for very complex queries, raw SQL (the SQL and MySQL posts) is still more expressive, and Prisma adds a build step and a learning curve of its own concepts. It also historically focused on relational databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite — all covered), with MongoDB support added later. The rule of thumb: Prisma for TypeScript apps where type safety and developer speed matter most; raw SQL or a query builder when queries get exotic or the project isn't TypeScript.

Takeaway

Prisma turns a readable schema into a type-safe database client, with migrations built in — so database mistakes become compile errors instead of production bugs. It is the modern default for TypeScript apps talking to relational databases.

Originally published at https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/prisma-explained-databases-without.html

articles.title: How I finally understood the Interface Segregation Principle
articles.description: The Intro   Letter four of five. Last post we broke a fat PaymentMethod into PaymentMethod +...
articles.body_html:
The Intro

Letter four of five. Last post we broke a fat PaymentMethod into PaymentMethod + Refundable and the compiler started catching our bugs. Today we take that idea and make it the whole show.

The I: Interface Segregation Principle. The one with the longest name and the shortest explanation.

The What

Official words:

No code should be forced to depend on methods it does not use.

That's... actually pretty readable for once. Let me still make it concrete.

An interface is a menu. ISP says: don't hand someone a 40-item menu when they came in for coffee. Give them the coffee menu.

Let's build a smart home to see what happens when the menu gets too big.

The How

We start with a lamp and a speaker. The team decides every device should implement one common interface so the app can treat them all the same. Reasonable!

// src/smart-device.ts
export interface SmartDevice {
  turnOn(): void
  turnOff(): void
  setTemperature(celsius: number): void
  play(track: string): void
  pause(): void
  setBrightness(percent: number): void
}

Now let's implement the lamp:

// src/lamp.ts
import type { SmartDevice } from './smart-device.js'

export class Lamp implements SmartDevice {
  private on = false

  turnOn() {
    this.on = true
    console.log('💡 lamp on')
  }

  turnOff() {
    this.on = false
    console.log('💡 lamp off')
  }

  setBrightness(percent: number) {
    console.log(`💡 brightness ${percent}%`)
  }

  setTemperature() {
    throw new Error('A lamp has no thermostat')
  }

  play() {
    throw new Error('A lamp cannot play music')
  }

  pause() {
    throw new Error('A lamp cannot pause music')
  }
}

Three real methods. Three methods that exist only to throw. The lamp is 50% apology.

The speaker is the same story in reverse: play() and pause() are real, setBrightness() and setTemperature() are throws. And the thermostat implements six methods to use one.

Now the app layer. We want a "good night" routine that turns everything off:

// src/routines.ts
import type { SmartDevice } from './smart-device.js'

export function goodNight(devices: SmartDevice[]) {
  for (const device of devices) {
    device.turnOff()
  }
}

Works. But then someone writes "movie mode":

export function movieMode(devices: SmartDevice[]) {
  for (const device of devices) {
    device.setBrightness(20)
    device.play('intro.mp3')
  }
}

Run it with a lamp in the list and play() throws. Run it with a speaker and setBrightness() throws. The function signature says "give me any SmartDevice" and that's a lie. If you read the last post, you just spotted a Liskov violation. ISP is how we stop creating them.

And one more pain you don't see until month three: add lockDoor() to SmartDevice for the new smart lock and every existing device, including the lamp, has to grow another throwing method. One interface change, twelve files touched. Ouch.

Step 1: split the menu by capability

What can devices actually do? Let's list the verbs and group them:

// src/capabilities.ts
export interface Switchable {
  turnOn(): void
  turnOff(): void
}

export interface Dimmable {
  setBrightness(percent: number): void
}

export interface Thermostat {
  setTemperature(celsius: number): void
}

export interface MediaPlayer {
  play(track: string): void
  pause(): void
}

Four tiny interfaces. Each one is a single idea.

Step 2: devices pick what they can honestly do 

// src/lamp.ts
import type { Switchable, Dimmable } from './capabilities.js'

export class Lamp implements Switchable, Dimmable {
  turnOn() {
    console.log('💡 lamp on')
  }

  turnOff() {
    console.log('💡 lamp off')
  }

  setBrightness(percent: number) {
    console.log(`💡 brightness ${percent}%`)
  }
}

// src/speaker.ts
import type { Switchable, MediaPlayer } from './capabilities.js'

export class Speaker implements Switchable, MediaPlayer {
  turnOn() {
    console.log('🔊 speaker on')
  }

  turnOff() {
    console.log('🔊 speaker off')
  }

  play(track: string) {
    console.log(`🔊 playing ${track}`)
  }

  pause() {
    console.log('🔊 paused')
  }
}

Zero throws. The lamp is 100% lamp.

Step 3: routines ask for the capability they use 

// src/routines.ts
import type { Switchable, Dimmable, MediaPlayer } from './capabilities.js'

export function goodNight(devices: Switchable[]) {
  for (const device of devices) {
    device.turnOff()
  }
}

export function movieMode(lights: Dimmable[], players: MediaPlayer[]) {
  for (const light of lights) {
    light.setBrightness(20)
  }
  for (const player of players) {
    player.play('intro.mp3')
  }
}

// src/main.ts
import { Lamp } from './lamp.js'
import { Speaker } from './speaker.js'
import { goodNight, movieMode } from './routines.js'

const lamp = new Lamp()
const speaker = new Speaker()

movieMode([lamp], [speaker])
goodNight([lamp, speaker])

Output:

💡 brightness 20%
🔊 playing intro.mp3
💡 lamp off
🔊 speaker off

Try to sneak the speaker into the lights array and TypeScript stops you before you even hit save. 🛑

Step 4: the smart lock test

New device, new capability:

// src/capabilities.ts
export interface Lockable {
  lock(): void
  unlock(): void
}

// src/door-lock.ts
import type { Lockable } from './capabilities.js'

export class DoorLock implements Lockable {
  lock() {
    console.log('🔒 locked')
  }

  unlock() {
    console.log('🔓 unlocked')
  }
}

Files touched besides the new ones: zero. The lamp didn't even blink.

The Why

  • No more apology methods. If a class throws "not supported", the interface was too fat. Split it until every implementation is honest.
  • Functions say exactly what they need. goodNight(devices: Switchable[]) tells you in the signature that it only flips switches. Documentation for free.
  • Adding a capability doesn't ripple. New interface, new class, done. Existing devices are untouched.
  • Tests get tiny. Want to test goodNight()? Pass an object with turnOn and turnOff. You don't need to fake six methods to test two.
  • It is cheap in TypeScript. Interfaces compile to nothing. Four small ones cost exactly as much as one big one: zero bytes.

Rule of thumb: if you can't describe an interface in one short sentence ("something you can switch on and off"), it's probably two interfaces.

The Goodbye

Four down. The final letter is the D, Dependency Inversion, and it's the one that ties the whole series together. If you've read my post about loosely coupled modules you already have a head start.

Until then: find an interface with more than five methods and ask it, politely, what it really wants to be. Happy coding 🤝

articles.title: 92 Green Field Tests Meant Nothing Until I Counted Which Could Lie
articles.description: The v0.2.0 field test for agentwatch ran 94 cases across 15 suites. 92 passed. 0 failed.  It was the...
articles.body_html:
The v0.2.0 field test for agentwatch ran 94 cases across 15 suites. 92 passed. 0 failed.

It was the least trustworthy green I'd ever shipped. Not because anything was failing — because I couldn't say why it was passing.

So I did a census. Of the 94 case assertions, how many could fail if the claim they were checking turned out to be false?

The answer was about 8.

The census

Every case had a step script. I read all 94 and sorted them into shapes:

Shape Count What it proves
Driver runs, prints ok: ..., exits 0 52 The commands executed
Container/service checks 16 The stack is up
Existence / syntax (test -f, json.tool) 11 The artifact exists and parses
Substring grep on own output 9 The word appears
python -c "import x" 5 The module loads
`... \ \ true`
Asserts a real condition ~8 The claim holds

That table is the whole finding. A suite where 8 of 94 assertions can fail isn't a test suite — it's a deployment script with extra steps. Every one of those 86 other cases would have stayed green with the feature broken, in many cases completely broken.

Two of the 92 greens were hiding exactly that: a Tempo backend that didn't exist, and a version banner that printed the wrong number. Both passed. Both were "plumbing green."

The method: four patterns, not 84 one-offs

Reading 94 cases sounds like a week of work. It was one evening, because the cases collapse into four patterns — and each pattern has one fix:

Pattern A — the shipped test already covers the plan condition. The single biggest surprise of the census: for something like 44 of the weak cases, the repo already had a canonical pytest module that asserts exactly what the field case was groping at. test_browser_verifier.py for the offline verifier, test_conformance_runner.py for the plugin API, test_access.py for the role matrix. The field case was doing test -f on a file while a real test sat two directories over.

The fix was one generic driver — shipped_tests.py, ~40 lines, which runs a named pytest module under the right PYTHONPATH and fails loudly if it doesn't pass. One driver, 44 cases grounded, zero re-implementation. If you take one thing from this post: before you write an assertion, grep your own test suite. The cheapest sufficient check usually already exists, and a hand-rolled one will drift from it.

Pattern B — the driver runs but its ok() is unconditional. The driver calls the real CLI, gets real JSON back, prints ok: ..., exits 0. Nothing ever looks inside the JSON. The fix is boring: parse it and assert the contract — the derivation version is present, the join summary carries the classified form, the statement is backed by a config key. The driver already had the data in its hand.

Pattern C — existence standing in for function. test -f verifier.html. json.tool bundle.json. import agentsec_agentwatch.conformance. Each of these has a real condition one step deeper, and each one got rewritten to it.

Pattern D — needs tooling that isn't in the room. Two cases need a real LangGraph SDK driver and two independent OSS parsers. No local fix exists. These stayed run-only, flagged, never faked — the report says "blocked" and names exactly what's missing. That's the fourth pattern's whole fix: honest labeling.

What grounding did to the failure count

Here's the uncomfortable, excellent part. Hardening didn't just make checks stronger — it made them fail. Three hardened cases went red on their first honest run:

  • A backend check that now queried Tempo — which was never started.
  • A matrix check that now asserted "no modeled Tier-1 rows" — one row was modeled.
  • A console accessibility check that now ran real axe rules — the page had no <main> landmark.

All three were product defects the old assertions couldn't see. Zero of them were test bugs. The green had been hiding them the entire time, and the only way any of them surfaced was by making an assertion able to fail.

That's the sentence I want to keep: you don't find bugs by running your suite, you find them by making your suite able to fail.

The bookkeeping that made it stick

Two small disciplines carried the campaign:

Every fix, re-run, before the report changes. Not "fixed in batch, verified later." One case, one run, one verdict on disk, then the report row updates. The report's totals are derived from verdict.json files, never from the summary JSON — stale summaries were exactly how earlier false greens hid.

A grounded/run-only tally in the report, not just PASS/FAIL. The final state reads 92 PASS / 0 FAIL / 1 declared / 1 N/A, and 90 of the 92 grounded. That second number is the one that took weeks. It's also the only number in the report I'd defend in an audit, because it's the only one with receipts per case.

Batches of 5, then 7 — same-shape cases together, one shared stack per batch, one commit per batch. Pattern-classification isn't just a reporting convenience; it's the difference between 84 one-off fixes and 4 fixes applied 84 times.

What I keep from this

  • A green suite answers "did it run." It takes deliberate work to make it answer "is it true."
  • Your repo's own test suite is the cheapest, least-drifty source of assertions. Grep it before writing any.
  • If a check can't fail, it will pass through anything — including the outage you wrote it to catch.
  • Blocked cases get labeled, not faked. The tally 90 grounded / 2 blocked is trustworthy because the 2 are named.

All of it is in the v0.2.0 field test report, shipped with agentwatch v0.2.1 — on PyPI.

The question worth taking to your own CI tonight: of your green suite, how many assertions could fail if their claim were false? If you don't know — that number is your suite's real size. Everything else is rehearsal.

References

  • Release: agentwatch v0.2.1 on GitHub · on PyPI
  • v0.2.0 field test report — the assertion-shape census, the four hardening patterns, and the per-case grounding tally
  • The generic driver that grounded 44 cases
  • The three defects hardening surfaced: FT-BACKEND-2 (Tempo), FT-MATRIX-1 (modeled Tier-1 row), FT-LUI-1 (console <main> landmark)
  • Suite: agentic-suite — the full set of agent-security tools

articles.title: Your CI Is Green. Can a Pull Request Steal Your Secrets?
articles.description: A new pull request arrives.  GitHub Actions starts a workflow. The tests pass. Everything looks...
articles.body_html:
A new pull request arrives.

GitHub Actions starts a workflow. The tests pass. Everything looks normal.

But a workflow can do more than run tests. Depending on its configuration, it may have access to repository secrets, a GitHub token, and other resources.

If that workflow executes code supplied by an untrusted contributor, a pull request can become a security problem before anyone merges it.

Here’s what every developer using GitHub Actions should check.

1. Understand the risky combination

The problem is not simply receiving a pull request.

The dangerous combination is:

  1. A workflow runs with elevated access.
  2. It checks out code from an untrusted pull request.
  3. It executes that code.

That code might run through a test command, a build script, a dependency installation, or a configuration file.

GitHub specifically warns about checking out and executing untrusted pull request code in privileged pull_request_target and workflow_run workflows.

2. Look closely at pull_request_target

pull_request_target can be useful for tasks such as labeling or commenting on a pull request.

But it runs in a privileged context associated with the base repository.

A risky pattern looks like this:

# Insecure example: do not copy
on: pull_request_target

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}

      - run: make test

The checkout retrieves the pull request’s code.

The next step executes its Makefile.

If that file was changed by an attacker, the commands run in the workflow’s context. GitHub documents this pattern and its risks.

Checking out code and executing code are different steps. The risk appears when untrusted code is run with privileges it shouldn’t have.

For ordinary pull request tests, consider using the pull_request event with minimal permissions. Check your repository’s settings and event behavior, especially when working with forks.

3. Treat pull request text as untrusted too

Code isn’t the only input a contributor controls.

A pull request title, description, branch name, or comment may also be untrusted.

Consider this pattern:

# Risky: the title is inserted directly into a shell script
- run: |
    title="${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"
    echo "$title"

GitHub evaluates the expression before the shell script runs. An unexpected title can change the generated script.

A safer pattern is to pass the value through an environment variable:

- name: Print the pull request title
  env:
    PR_TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}
  run: |
    printf '%s\n' "$PR_TITLE"

The value is now handled as data by the shell in this example. Still avoid using it in eval or another command that interprets its contents as code.

GitHub’s security guidance recommends this intermediate-variable approach for inline scripts.

4. Give workflows only the permissions they need

Does a test job need permission to write to your repository?

If it only needs to read code, start with limited permissions:

permissions:
  contents: read

Then grant additional permissions only to jobs that require them.

Also review which secrets each job receives. A workflow that doesn’t need a deployment credential shouldn’t have access to one.

Smaller permissions reduce the impact if something goes wrong.

5. Check third-party actions

An action in your workflow is code that runs as part of your CI process.

Review what it does and what access its job has. For stronger protection against a tag being changed, GitHub recommends pinning third-party actions to a full commit SHA and verifying that the SHA belongs to the expected repository.

Also keep pinned actions updated through a deliberate review process. Pinning an old vulnerable version doesn’t make it safe.

6. Don’t assume masked logs protect secrets

GitHub can redact known secrets from logs. That helps prevent accidental exposure.

But log masking is not a security boundary. Malicious code with access to a secret may send it elsewhere rather than simply print it.

The stronger question is:

“Does this job need access to the secret at all?”

GitHub makes the same distinction in its guidance on compromised runners.

7. Review your workflows today

Open your repository’s .github/workflows directory and check:

  • Which workflows use pull_request_target or workflow_run?
  • Do privileged jobs check out and run pull request code?
  • Can untrusted text become part of a shell script?
  • Which jobs have write permissions?
  • Which jobs receive secrets?
  • Are third-party actions reviewed and pinned?
  • Does untrusted code run on a persistent self-hosted runner?

If you find a questionable workflow, trace what it actually executes—including scripts and dependencies—not just the YAML file.

The question behind the green check

A green CI badge tells you that the checks reported success.

It doesn’t tell you whether the workflow had the right permissions or safely handled untrusted input.

Before approving your next pull request, ask:

“What can this workflow execute—and what can that code access?”

That question can reveal problems a passing test suite never will.

Have you reviewed the permissions and triggers in your GitHub Actions workflows recently?

Further reading:

  • GitHub: Secure use of GitHub Actions
  • GitHub: Securely using pull_request_target
  • GitHub: Script injection in workflows

articles.title: console.log is a legitimate debugging tool
articles.description: I've used breakpoints, profilers, and all the fancy devtools. But when something breaks at 1 AM, my...
articles.body_html:
I've used breakpoints, profilers, and all the fancy devtools. But when something breaks at 1 AM, my first move is still:

console.log("here");
console.log("here 2");
console.log("WHY IS THIS UNDEFINED");

It's not pretty, but it works. Here's what I've noticed over time:

  • Writing a log forces me to state what I expect. To log a value, I first have to decide what it should be at that line.
  • It works everywhere. Every language, every stack, zero setup.
  • The bug often shows up while I'm typing the log. Half the time I find it before running anything.

Where it stops working

The rule I follow now: if I've added more than 5 logs, I'm guessing, not debugging.

At that point the logs have stopped answering questions and started adding noise. That's the moment to stop and step through the code with a real debugger, where I can inspect state, watch the call stack, and see exactly where the value changes.

Print debugging isn't the problem

Used on purpose, console.log is a fast way to test a hypothesis. The trouble starts when it replaces thinking.

Print debugging isn't the problem. Not knowing when to stop is.

articles.title: Getting Your First 10 Users Is Harder Than Building the Product (Or Is It?)
articles.description: TL;DR: Building proves you can create a solution. Finding users proves the solution matters to...
articles.body_html:
TL;DR: Building proves you can create a solution. Finding users proves the solution matters to someone. These are separate questions, and finishing the first never answers the second.

Reading time: about 12 minutes. For developers and first-time founders.

A developer can spend six months building a product without having to convince a single stranger to care about it.

The code either works or it doesn't. A bug can be investigated. A slow query can be measured. If a feature breaks, there's usually somewhere to start looking.

Then the product is ready, the landing page is live, and the founder starts reaching out to people.

Nothing happens.

A few people visit the website. Someone says the idea sounds interesting. A friend offers encouragement. Perhaps a handful of people create accounts, but nobody returns the following week.

Suddenly, the problem that seemed straightforward during development becomes difficult to explain. The product exists. The founder believes it solves a real problem. Yet the people who supposedly need it aren't showing up.

This is where a familiar piece of startup advice enters the conversation: getting your first ten users is harder than building the product.

There is a reason the advice resonates, especially with developers who are building their first businesses. But it also leaves an important question unanswered.

The real question

Is finding those first ten users actually harder than building the product, or does it feel harder because founders have less control over what happens next?

The distinction matters. If you misunderstand why people aren't using your product, you can spend months trying to solve the wrong problem.

Jump to a section
  1. Building gives you feedback. Selling gives you silence.
  2. Stripe's early customers didn't arrive through a signup page
  3. Ten signups can still mean zero real users
  4. When the advice is right, and when it isn't
  5. A quiet launch can mean four different things
  6. What should you actually do to find the first ten?
  7. The first ten are not the finish line

1. Building gives you feedback. Selling gives you silence.

Consider what happens when a developer encounters a difficult technical problem.

The solution might take hours, days, or even weeks. But there is usually a way to investigate it. You can inspect the logs, reproduce the failure, test a different approach, and gradually narrow down the possibilities.

Progress isn't guaranteed, but the work often produces information you can use.

Customer acquisition is different.

You send twenty carefully written messages and receive two replies. You publish a detailed explanation of your product and nobody clicks through. You demonstrate a feature to someone who says they would love to use it, then never hear from them again.

You have an outcome, but you don't necessarily know what caused it.

Perhaps the people you contacted don't have the problem. Perhaps they do, but your message arrived at the wrong time. Perhaps the product is useful but switching to it would take too much effort. Perhaps they simply don't trust an unfamiliar founder with something important to their work.

Those explanations require different responses. Silence alone cannot tell you which one is correct.

This is one reason acquisition can feel more frustrating than development. With code, you can often make the next experiment more specific because you understand the system you're investigating. With customers, you are still learning how the system works.

You are learning what people care about, what they already use, what they will pay to change, and what makes them trust a product they have never tried.

And you are learning all of this while trying to persuade them to give you their time.

That is a genuinely difficult problem. But it isn't necessarily a harder problem in every measurable sense. A technically ambitious product might require years of engineering, while a simple product could find its first customers in a few days.

The more useful distinction:

Building tests... Finding customers tests...
The question Can you create the solution? Does the solution matter enough that someone will act on it?
Feedback you get Logs, errors, measurable results Often silence
Who controls the outcome Mostly you Mostly other people

Those are separate questions, and finishing the first does not answer the second.

2. Stripe's early customers didn't arrive through a signup page

In his 2013 essay Do Things That Don't Scale, Paul Graham describes how Patrick and John Collison acquired early users for Stripe.1

When somebody agreed to try the payment integration, the brothers wouldn't simply send a link and wait. They would ask to borrow the person's laptop and help install it immediately.

Y Combinator came to call this the "Collison installation."

The approach seems almost excessive now. Why should a founder personally install a product when the whole point of software is to make the experience repeatable?

Because the founders were solving a problem that a signup page couldn't solve for them.

A person who agrees to try a product has made a relatively inexpensive commitment. They can change their mind without consequence. Actually installing it requires more effort and brings the product into contact with the person's real workflow.

By helping with the installation, the founders removed friction and discovered what happened when someone tried to use Stripe for real.

Context matters. Stripe was addressing a concrete problem for developers and businesses, and its early founders had access to a network of potential customers through the startup ecosystem. Their approach does not prove that every product can acquire customers by offering personal onboarding.

It does show something more practical: sometimes the obstacle between interest and usage is not a lack of awareness. It is the work required to get started.

What that looks like in practice:

  • Developer tool: help someone integrate it
  • Software for accountants: import a customer's existing data
  • A service: deliver the first result personally before asking for a longer commitment

These approaches do not scale indefinitely. That is precisely why they can be valuable at the beginning.

Before automating an onboarding process, a founder needs to understand where people struggle with it. Before spending heavily on marketing, they need to know what happens after somebody responds.

The first ten customers can be valuable for the revenue they bring in. They can also reveal problems that a founder working alone would never have discovered.

3. Ten signups can still mean zero real users

There is another problem with the way founders talk about their first users: the word user can describe several very different situations.

  1. Someone visits the landing page.
  2. Someone else joins the waitlist.
  3. A third person creates an account, opens the dashboard, and leaves.

All three might appear in a growth report. None necessarily demonstrates that the product is delivering its promised value.

This distinction is more than a matter of terminology.

In his account of Superhuman's product-market-fit process, founder Rahul Vohra described a company that had spent years building its email product but still needed a clearer way to measure whether users genuinely valued it.2

Superhuman surveyed people who had used the product at least twice in the preceding two weeks. It asked how they would feel if they could no longer use it.

Only 22% said they would be very disappointed.

That result mattered because these weren't simply people who had heard about Superhuman. They had already experienced the product. Yet most did not consider it indispensable.

The team used the survey responses to identify the people who valued the product most, understand what those people appreciated, and make improvements intended to strengthen product-market fit. Vohra subsequently reported that the score rose from 22% to 58%.

- 22%  "very disappointed"  (before)
+ 58%  "very disappointed"  (after)

58%−22%=36 percentage points 58\% - 22\% = 36 \text{ percentage points} 58%−22%=36 percentage points

What this example does and doesn't establish

There are limits to what this example establishes. The survey is a useful diagnostic, not a universal scientific test that can independently prove product-market fit. The results came from Superhuman's particular audience and product, and a high score does not guarantee a sustainable business.

Still, the underlying problem is important.

Getting somebody to sign up and getting somebody to care whether your product disappears are not the same achievement.

For a founder trying to find ten users, this means the milestone needs a definition.

Ten registered accounts might be an appropriate early milestone for testing whether people will respond to an offer. Ten people who repeatedly use a core feature tell you something different. Ten paying customers tell you something different again.

None of those numbers is automatically the right target. The right target depends on what the product is supposed to accomplish.

Product type A meaningful signal might be
Tool used every morning Returning frequently
Quarterly accounting software Completing the quarterly task (daily usage would be a strange expectation)
One-time service Successful completion and willingness to recommend the provider

A founder should measure the behaviour that demonstrates value, rather than assume every product needs the same pattern of engagement.

Read the Superhuman product-market-fit story

4. When the advice is right, and when it isn't

The claim that customer acquisition is harder than building is most convincing when a founder has a working product but no reliable way to reach people who need it.

Imagine a developer who builds a scheduling tool for freelance designers. The technical work is manageable. The product works. But the developer has no existing audience among designers, no relationships with design agencies, and no idea where these freelancers look for tools.

The product might be finished in a month. Finding a group of people willing to try it, learning what they actually need, and discovering whether any of them will pay could take much longer.

The developer isn't necessarily struggling because the product is bad. They are trying to solve a problem for a group of people they don't yet understand well enough.

Now consider a different founder: an accountant who builds a small tool to automate a tedious task that several existing clients already complain about. The founder knows the workflow, has access to the intended users, and can test the tool with people who experience the problem every week.

The technical challenge could be the hardest part of that business. Finding the first few users might be comparatively straightforward.

Developer building for designers Accountant building for own clients
Existing audience No Yes
Knows the workflow No Yes
Likely hardest part Finding users Building the tool

Neither example is unusual enough to support a universal rule. Together, they show why the headline depends on the founder, the market, and the product.

Existing distribution changes the equation, too. Someone with an established audience, a respected reputation in a niche, or a network of potential buyers isn't starting from the same position as someone nobody knows.

That advantage is real. It doesn't mean their product is better, or that their acquisition strategy is automatically repeatable. It means some of the work required to earn attention happened before the product was launched.

The same qualification applies to technically novel products. If a founder doesn't yet know whether a proposed system can work at an acceptable cost, speed, or level of reliability, engineering experiments may need to come first. Talking to potential customers cannot resolve every question about technical feasibility.

The mistake is treating either building or customer acquisition as the correct first step for every startup.

Sometimes the founder needs to write more code. Sometimes they need to speak to potential customers before writing another line. Often, they need to do both, using what they learn from one to inform the other.

5. A quiet launch can mean four different things

Suppose you launch your product and, after several weeks, you still haven't found ten meaningful users.

The tempting response is to do more marketing. Post in more communities. Send more messages. Try another launch platform.

That might help. But first, consider where the process is breaking.

flowchart LR
    A[Launch] --> B{Right people<br/>seeing it?}
    B -- No --> C[1. Reach problem]
    B -- Yes --> D{Taking the<br/>next step?}
    D -- No --> E[2. Offer problem]
    D -- Yes --> F{Reaching the<br/>main benefit?}
    F -- No --> G[3. Activation problem]
    F -- Yes --> H{Returning<br/>or paying?}
    H -- No --> I[4. Retention problem]
    H -- Yes --> J[Keep going]

1. The right people aren't seeing the product

Perhaps the product solves a genuine problem, but your potential customers don't spend time on the channels you're using. Or perhaps you're targeting such a broad audience that your message never feels relevant to anyone in particular.

In this case, changing the product may accomplish very little. You need to understand where the intended customers already look for solutions and how to reach them.

2. People see the product but don't take the next step

This could mean the value proposition is unclear. It could also mean the problem isn't urgent, the price is too high, the proposed solution feels risky, or the person reading your message doesn't have the authority to make a purchase.

It is worth asking what your offer requires someone to believe before they act. An unfamiliar product asking for access to sensitive business data has a much larger trust problem than a free tool that works entirely in the browser.

3. People try the product but never reach its main benefit

Perhaps setup takes too long. Maybe the first screen asks users to configure five things before they can accomplish anything useful. The product might even work exactly as intended, but the value isn't apparent to a new user.

This is where watching someone use the product can reveal more than another round of promotional posts.

4. People get value once but don't return or pay

This is the most uncomfortable possibility because the founder has evidence that the product can work for someone, yet the behaviour isn't continuing.

The problem might be retention, pricing, a low-frequency need, or a mismatch between the person using the product and the person expected to pay. It could also mean the product is useful but not important enough to replace an existing habit.

Not a complete diagnosis. These four categories aren't exhaustive, and the boundaries between them aren't always clean. A confusing product can look like a marketing problem. A weak offer can look like a distribution problem. Low retention can reflect a product that works perfectly but solves a problem people rarely encounter.

The point is not to label every failure immediately.

It is to stop treating every failure as the same failure.

6. What should you actually do to find the first ten?

The best starting point is smaller than a launch campaign.

Choose a specific group of people who already experience the problem your product is intended to solve. Be precise enough that you can identify actual individuals, rather than an enormous category of potential customers.

Then investigate what they do today.

If you're building invoice software for freelancers, find out how those freelancers currently create invoices, follow up on unpaid bills, and keep track of their income. Ask what happens when the process goes wrong. Look for examples of real frustration, time lost, money lost, or workarounds people have already built.

Steve Blank's writing on customer development makes a useful distinction here: founders begin with hypotheses about customers and their needs, then test those hypotheses through conversations and experiments.3 The goal is to discover what is true, not simply to collect encouraging responses.

That means asking about actual behaviour is usually more informative than asking whether somebody likes your idea.

Example: weak evidence vs. strong evidence

A person may tell you they would happily use an invoicing tool. That costs them nothing.

Finding out what they currently use, whether they have paid for alternatives, and whether they'll try your product with a real invoice gives you stronger evidence.

Once you understand the problem, offer a small, concrete next step.

Don't necessarily ask someone to adopt your entire product. Ask whether they'll try one feature, bring one real task into it, or spend twenty minutes showing you how they currently handle the problem.

If the product is ready, help them use it. If it isn't, a prototype or a manually delivered version of the service might be enough to test the underlying assumption, provided you don't misrepresent what you've built.

Track what happens next

Stage What to record
Reached Did the intended person actually see the offer?
Responded Did they reply or ask a meaningful question?
Tried Did they attempt the real task?
Activated Did they reach the product's core value?
Returned Did they use it again when the need arose?
Committed Did they pay, renew, recommend it, or make another meaningful commitment?

Not every product needs all six stages, and not every commitment looks like a payment. The table is a way to make the process observable, not a universal funnel that every business must follow.

Keep notes on why people stop, preferably in their own words. A polite refusal and a detailed objection are not equivalent. Neither is the same as someone who tries the product, gets value from it, and simply doesn't need it again until next month.

Then choose the next experiment based on what you learned:

  • [ ] The wrong people are seeing the offer: change the audience or channel
  • [ ] The right people understand the offer but don't care enough to try it: investigate the problem and the value proposition
  • [ ] They try the product but fail to reach its main benefit: work on that experience
  • [ ] They get value but don't return or pay: investigate the frequency, importance, and economics of the problem

Two weeks can be enough to uncover useful patterns when the target customers are accessible and the product delivers value quickly. It may be nowhere near enough for a business with a long sales cycle or a problem that occurs only a few times a year.

The objective isn't to promise ten users within fourteen days. It is to finish the experiment knowing more than you did when you started.

7. The first ten are not the finish line

There is a reason founders remember their first users. Each one represents a decision that happened outside the codebase: somebody noticed the product, considered it relevant, decided to try it, and perhaps found enough value to return.

But the number ten can be misleading.

Ten users who... ...might tell you
signed up because a friend asked Very little about whether strangers will pay
independently share the same painful problem and pay to solve it A great deal
never return A product problem that another hundred signups would only make harder to ignore

The work isn't finished when the tenth person arrives. That's often when the next question becomes possible.

  • Can you find another ten people with the same problem?
  • Can you reach them through a process you understand?
  • Do they experience enough value to keep using the product?
  • Does acquiring and serving them make economic sense?

Those questions are harder to answer than whether a product can attract ten signups, and they matter more to the future of the business.

So, is getting your first ten users harder than building the product?

Sometimes. Especially when the founder understands the technology but knows very little about the people who might buy it. But the comparison becomes less useful when it turns into a universal rule, or when it encourages founders to treat engineering and customer discovery as competing activities.

A product can be technically excellent and commercially irrelevant. It can also be commercially promising before its engineering is finished. The difficult work is finding out which situation you're in while there is still time to change direction.

That begins with a more useful question than how to get ten users.

Your next question

What would you need to learn from the next person who tries your product to know what to do next?

Share your answer in the comments.

The Startup Café — Real Startup Lessons. Beyond the Hype.

  1. Paul Graham, "Do Things That Don't Scale," 2013. The essay is where the Collison installation story comes from. ↩

  2. Rahul Vohra's account on the First Round Review. The 22% and 58% figures come from Superhuman's own survey of its own users, so treat them as one company's data point. ↩

  3. Steve Blank's customer development writing is a collection of posts, so start with the ones on customer discovery and hypothesis testing. ↩

articles.title: Minifying Astro HTML after the build: a post-build script, measured
articles.description: This is a standalone example for static Astro projects. The site where I measured it,...
articles.body_html:
This is a standalone example for static Astro projects. The site where I measured it, straffesites.com, does not use the script in production. In October 2026, I did run it on a copy of that site's build to measure what a post-build step does to your Astro HTML. The script adds unique IDs to headings that do not have one yet and minifies the files with html-minifier-terser. Here is how to set it up, what the measurement showed, and what to watch out for.

What do you need to get started?

Before you start, make sure you have the following installed:

  • Node.js (version 22.12.0 or later for Astro 7)
  • Astro (version 5 or later)

Installing the dependencies

The script depends on three packages: globby, html-minifier-terser, and jsdom. Install them as development dependencies:

npm install --save-dev globby html-minifier-terser jsdom

The process-html.mjs script

Create a file named process-html.mjs in the root of your Astro project. The code below uses Astro's default static output folder, dist. If you configured another output directory, adjust the path variable.

import fs from 'node:fs/promises'
import { globby } from 'globby'
import { minify } from 'html-minifier-terser'
import { JSDOM } from 'jsdom'

// Find all HTML files in the output folder
const path = './dist'
const files = await globby(`${path}/**/*.html`)

await Promise.all(
  files.map(async (file) => {
    console.log('Processing file:', file)
    let html = await fs.readFile(file, 'utf-8')

    // Preserve existing IDs and add unique IDs to other h2, h3 and h4 elements
    const dom = new JSDOM(html)
    const headings = dom.window.document.querySelectorAll('h2, h3, h4')
    const usedIds = new Set(
      [...dom.window.document.querySelectorAll('[id]')].map((element) => element.id)
    )

    for (const heading of headings) {
      if (heading.id) continue

      const baseId = heading.textContent
        .normalize('NFKD')
        .replace(/\p{Mark}+/gu, '')
        .trim()
        .toLowerCase()
        .replace(/[^\p{Letter}\p{Number}]+/gu, '-')
        .replace(/^-|-$/g, '') || 'section'

      let id = baseId
      let suffix = 2
      while (usedIds.has(id)) id = `${baseId}-${suffix++}`

      heading.setAttribute('id', id)
      usedIds.add(id)
    }

    html = dom.serialize()

    // Minify the resulting HTML
    html = await minify(html, {
      removeComments: false,
      preserveLineBreaks: true,
      collapseWhitespace: true,
    })

    await fs.writeFile(file, html)
  })
)

Updating package.json

Update package.json to run the script after the build. Add && node process-html.mjs after astro build, as shown below.

{
  "name": "astro-process-html",
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "astro dev",
    "start": "astro dev",
    "build": "astro build && node process-html.mjs",
    "preview": "astro preview",
    "astro": "astro"
  }
}

What does it change in practice?

I ran the script above exactly as shown on a copy of the straffesites.com build: 236 HTML pages, built with Astro 7.2.8 and the default compressHTML setting. The package versions were globby 16.2.4, html-minifier-terser 7.2.0, and jsdom 30.1.2. The result is the opposite of what you might expect: the Astro HTML did not get smaller, it got larger.

Measurement Before the script After the script Difference
All 236 HTML files 31,807,539 bytes 32,067,896 bytes +0.82%
Same files with gzip 6,573,834 bytes 6,637,927 bytes +0.97%
Same files with Brotli 5,506,134 bytes 5,562,603 bytes +1.03%
Heading IDs added – 6,552 on 236 pages on every page

Two steps explain it. The minify step alone, with the same options, removed 408 bytes across the whole build, because Astro had already cleaned up the whitespace. Parsing and serializing with jsdom alone made the files 38,059 bytes larger, partly because jsdom writes every empty attribute in full (data-site-header becomes data-site-header=""). The rest comes from the new IDs. Processing took 25.7 seconds.

The Astro documentation explains why compressHTML already does so much:

"Since v7.0, Astro applies by default the JSX whitespace rules used by frameworks like React."

— Astro, Configuration Reference: compressHTML

So the value of the script is in the transformation, not in bytes. Every h2, h3, and h4 gets a stable, unique anchor ID, so you can link to any section. Existing IDs stay in place. The example does not remove empty paragraphs or CMS attributes; that needs extra, tested logic. Measure your own build to decide whether the anchors are worth the extra bytes.

Which pitfalls should you know about?

Keep HTML comments when using Svelte 5 or other comment-based hydration. That is why this example sets removeComments: false. See the Svelte 5 migration guide.

  • Put the script in your build pipeline rather than running it manually. Every build overwrites the output folder, so the next deploy would discard a manual run. That is why package.json includes it above.
  • Keep preserveLineBreaks: true enabled. Without it, your HTML collapses onto one line, which makes built files much harder to diff or debug.
  • jsdom parses and serializes every page again. That is usually safe for ordinary HTML, but test hydrated Svelte or other framework islands whenever you extend the script.
  • collapseWhitespace can remove a visible space around inline elements in some edge cases. Check the design after the first run, especially around buttons and icons next to text.
  • Do not expect smaller files. jsdom writes empty attributes in full and every new ID costs bytes, so on an Astro 7 build your HTML is more likely to grow. Use the script for the anchors, not for the file size.

Is there an alternative to a standalone script?

If you only want smaller files and no heading anchors, you do not need to write anything yourself. An existing integration such as @playform/compress runs html-minifier-terser together with minifiers for CSS, JavaScript, SVG, and images in your Astro build. Measure the difference there too, because Astro has already compressed most of the HTML.

If you prefer an Astro integration to a standalone npm script, wrap the same logic in one. It runs on the astro:build:done hook and receives the output directory, so you do not have to hardcode paths. The integration is more reusable but slightly more involved: a standalone script is fine for one site, while an integration pays off across several projects.

This is only the integration skeleton, not a second complete script. Add the file processing above and convert the dir URL with fileURLToPath from node:url before using it as a globby path. Do not enable this alternative together with the npm post-build script.

// astro.config.mjs
import { defineConfig } from 'astro/config'

function processHtml() {
  return {
    name: 'process-html',
    hooks: {
      'astro:build:done': async ({ dir }) => {
        // Run the same globby and minification logic as process-html.mjs,
        // using every .html file in the output directory.
      },
    },
  }
}

export default defineConfig({
  integrations: [processHtml()],
})

Both approaches do the same thing: after the build, they process every HTML file. Choose the one that best fits how you manage projects.

Conclusion

With a few lines after the build, all your Astro HTML gets stable heading anchors on every deploy. You will not get smaller files: Astro already compresses the HTML, and on the measured site the build grew 0.82%. Use the script for a specific transformation and measure the effect on your own build.

The html-minifier-terser reference covers the remaining configuration options.

Originally published on straffesites.com.

articles.title: Your "use server" Functions Are Public HTTP Endpoints (And Middleware Won't Save You)
articles.description: Adding "use server" makes a TypeScript function look private, but it actually exposes a public HTTP POST endpoint. Learn the 3 mistakes that leave React and Next.js Server Actions vulnerable and how to fix them.
articles.body_html:
If you import a 'use server' function into a protected React component and pass it a typed TypeScript object, it looks and feels like a private, internal function call.

It isn't. Every exported 'use server' function in your codebase is compiled into a publicly reachable HTTP POST endpoint. Anyone with your action's identifier can invoke it directly from curl, Postman, or an automated script—with any JSON payload they want, completely bypassing your UI and often bypassing the authentication checks you thought were protecting it.

If your team treats Server Actions like regular TypeScript functions instead of public REST endpoints, your production app likely has an unauthenticated mutation or an authorization bug waiting to be discovered.

The Illusion: Why Developers Write Vulnerable Actions

Look at this common pattern in a modern Next.js App Router codebase:

// app/dashboard/billing/page.tsx (Protected by Layout)
import { requireAdminSession } from '@/lib/auth';
import { issueRefund } from '@/app/actions/billing';

export default async function BillingPage() {
  // ✅ The developer checks authentication in the Page or Layout
  const session = await requireAdminSession();

  return (
    <form action={async () => {
      'use server';
      await issueRefund({ invoiceId: 'inv_9921', amountCents: 5000 });
    }}>
      <button type="submit">Issue $50 Refund</button>
    </form>
  );
}

And here is the action file it imports:

// app/actions/billing.ts
'use server';

import { db } from '@/lib/db';

interface RefundInput {
  invoiceId: string;
  amountCents: number;
}

// ❌ CRITICAL VULNERABILITY: Publicly callable POST endpoint!
export async function issueRefund(input: RefundInput) {
  await db.invoices.update({
    where: { id: input.invoiceId },
    data: { status: 'REFUNDED', refundedAmount: input.amountCents },
  });

  return { success: true };
}

During code review, almost everyone approves this. The reasoning seems obvious:

  1. BillingPage calls requireAdminSession() before rendering the button.
  2. issueRefund requires a strongly typed RefundInput object.
  3. No API route (app/api/.../route.ts) was ever created.

Every single one of those assumptions fails at runtime.


The Golden Rule of Server Functions: Adding 'use server' does not create a private server helper. It instructs the bundler to register an HTTP POST handler backed by the React Flight protocol and assign it a public Next-Action hash.

Mistake #1: Assuming Layouts or Parent Pages Protect Server Actions

When a user navigates to /dashboard/billing, Next.js renders layout.tsx and page.tsx. If you placed your requireAdminSession() check inside layout.tsx, unauthenticated visitors get redirected before seeing the UI.

However, when a client invokes a Server Action, Next.js does not execute the parent layout.tsx rendering logic as an authorization gate before running the action. A Server Action is an independent entry point.

Furthermore, relying solely on edge middleware (middleware.ts or proxy.ts in Next.js 16) is an anti-pattern. Edge routing layers are designed for optimistic redirects and request shaping—not as your sole data-access security boundary. Even if your middleware blocks /dashboard/*, a Server Action can be POSTed to any route in your application that accepts POST requests if the attacker sends the Next-Action header, or if matcher rules miss an unprotected path.

How an attacker triggers a "use server" function with curl
When your client bundle loads, the hashed action IDs are embedded right inside the JavaScript chunks served to the browser. Anyone inspecting the network tab or static JS files can grab the 40-character Next-Action hash and send a raw HTTP request:
curl -X POST https://your-app.com/login \
  -H "Accept: text/x-component" \
  -H "Content-Type: text/plain;charset=UTF-8" \
  -H "Next-Action: 409a8b7c6d5e4f3a2b1c0d9e8f7a6b5c4d3e2f1a" \
  -d '[{"invoiceId":"inv_9921","amountCents":9999999}]'

Notice that the request targets /login (a public route) while passing the Next-Action header for issueRefund. Without an explicit session check inside issueRefund itself, the database mutation executes immediately.


Mistake #2: Trusting TypeScript Types at Runtime

In our vulnerable issueRefund(input: RefundInput) example, the developer typed amountCents: number.

TypeScript types are completely erased during compilation. When an HTTP request hits a Server Action endpoint, the React Server Components (RSC) Flight deserializer parses the raw request body and passes whatever the caller sent directly into your function's arguments.

An attacker can send:

  • Negative numbers ({"amountCents": -500000})
  • Unexpected types ({"invoiceId": {"$ne": null}, "amountCents": "NaN"})
  • Massive multi-megabyte strings designed to block your event loop or bloat database columns

Even worse, framework-level deserialization bugs—such as the critical CVE-2025-55182 (CVSS 10.0) in React Server Components and CVE-2025-66478 in Next.js, followed by the May 2026 Flight parser DoS advisories—proved that Server Function endpoints sit directly on the untrusted network perimeter.

Mistake #3: Accidental Export Exposure in "use server" Files

When you put 'use server' at the top of a file (app/actions/users.ts), every single export in that file becomes a public HTTP endpoint—even internal helper functions you only exported so you could unit-test them or call them from another server file!

// app/actions/users.ts
'use server';

// ❌ You exported this only for a unit test or another server module,
// but because the file has 'use server' at the top, this is now a public endpoint!
export async function dangerouslyResetUserQuota(userId: string) {
  await db.quotas.update({ where: { userId }, data: { used: 0 } });
}

If a function does not need to be invoked directly from a Client Component or HTML <form>, never export it from a 'use server' file. Move shared server logic into a plain .ts Data Access Layer (DAL) marked with import 'server-only'.

The Production Fix: Harden Every Action Boundary

To make Server Actions safe in production, treat every 'use server' function exactly like a public POST /api/* webhook. Every action must enforce three rules inside its own body:

  1. Authenticate inside the action (never trust layouts or middleware).
  2. Validate the runtime payload with a schema (such as Zod or Valibot) using unknown as the TypeScript parameter type.
  3. Verify resource ownership (Authorization / IDOR check) before mutating data.

Here is the hardened, production-ready pattern:

// app/actions/billing.ts
'use server';

import { z } from 'zod';
import { db } from '@/lib/db';
import { getVerifiedSession } from '@/lib/dal/auth';

// 1. Define a strict runtime validation schema
const RefundSchema = z.object({
  invoiceId: z.string().uuid(),
  amountCents: z.number().int().positive().max(100_000_00),
});

// 2. Type the input as `unknown` so TypeScript forces you to parse it first
export async function issueRefund(rawInput: unknown) {
  // Step A: Authenticate inside the action itself
  const session = await getVerifiedSession();
  if (!session || session.user.role !== 'BILLING_ADMIN') {
    throw new Error('Unauthorized');
  }

  // Step B: Validate runtime types and constraints
  const parsed = RefundSchema.safeParse(rawInput);
  if (!parsed.success) {
    return { ok: false, error: 'Invalid refund payload' };
  }

  const { invoiceId, amountCents } = parsed.data;

  // Step C: Enforce tenant/object ownership (Prevent IDOR)
  const updated = await db.invoices.updateMany({
    where: {
      id: invoiceId,
      organizationId: session.user.organizationId, // Scope to caller's org!
      status: 'PAID',
    },
    data: {
      status: 'REFUNDED',
      refundedAmount: amountCents,
    },
  });

  if (updated.count === 0) {
    return { ok: false, error: 'Invoice not found or not eligible' };
  }

  return { ok: true };
}

Read the Official Next.js Data Security and Server Actions Architecture Guide

Quick Production Audit Checklist

Run through this checklist on your repository today:

  • [ ] Search your codebase for 'use server' and inspect every export async function.
  • [ ] Remove export from any helper function inside a 'use server' file that shouldn't be callable from the browser, or move it to a server-only Data Access Layer.
  • [ ] Ensure every exported Server Action calls your session/authentication verification inside its own function body.
  • [ ] Replace trusted TypeScript parameter types with rawInput: unknown + runtime schema parsing (zod or valibot).
  • [ ] Scope every database UPDATE and DELETE query by the authenticated user's userId or organizationId to prevent IDOR.
  • [ ] Keep react, react-dom, and next patched against React Flight protocol advisories (such as CVE-2025-55182 and CVE-2026-23870) and enforce request body size limits at your reverse proxy or WAF.

The Takeaway

The ergonomics of React Server Actions are their greatest strength and their biggest security trap. By erasing the visual boundary between client code and server execution, 'use server' makes network boundaries invisible.

Never assume a layout, middleware redirect, or TypeScript interface protects a Server Action. If a file says 'use server', every exported function is a public HTTP endpoint—authenticate it, validate its payload at runtime, and authorize every database query inside the action itself.

Have you audited the 'use server' files in your production codebase recently—and did you find any exported functions missing an internal auth or schema check?

  • OWASP Top 10: A01 Broken Access Control & Insecure Direct Object References

articles.title: How to Divide Work Across Threads in JavaScript: CPU Cores, Workload, and Smart Scheduling
articles.description: Modern applications often need to process millions of records, generate reports, analyze events,...
articles.body_html:
Modern applications often need to process millions of records, generate reports, analyze events, resize images, or perform complex calculations. As workloads grow, running everything on a single JavaScript thread can become a performance bottleneck.

The solution isn't simply to create more threads. The real challenge is deciding how many threads to create, how to divide the work, and how to assign tasks efficiently based on the machine's available resources.

In this guide, we'll explore how JavaScript multithreading works in Node.js, how to divide workloads across CPU cores, and how to design a worker system that can scale efficiently.

1. Understanding JavaScript's Execution Model

JavaScript traditionally executes application code on a single main thread. In Node.js, this thread runs the event loop, handles callbacks, and coordinates asynchronous operations.

Consider a program that processes a large dataset:

function processData(records) {
  for (const record of records) {
    // Perform expensive calculations
  }
}

processData(largeDataset);

If processData() performs CPU-intensive work, the main thread remains occupied until the function finishes. During that time, other JavaScript callbacks cannot execute on the same thread.

As a result, an application may become unresponsive, requests may take longer to complete, and overall throughput can decrease.

Node.js provides the worker_threads module to run JavaScript in separate threads. These workers can execute CPU-intensive tasks in parallel, subject to the machine's available CPU resources.

The important distinction is that asynchronous programming and multithreading solve different problems:

  • Asynchronous programming allows a thread to continue while waiting for operations such as network or file I/O.
  • Multithreading allows JavaScript code to execute on multiple threads, making parallel CPU computation possible.

Understanding this distinction is the first step toward building an efficient worker system.

2. How Does a Machine Determine Its Thread Capacity?

Before distributing work, we need to understand the machine running the application.

Imagine a server with the following specifications:

Resource Specification
Logical CPUs 8
RAM 16 GB
Workload CPU-intensive data processing
Main thread Handles coordination and application logic

The eight logical CPUs represent the hardware's reported capacity for simultaneous thread execution. Depending on the processor, logical CPUs may include simultaneous multithreading, such as Intel Hyper-Threading.

However, eight logical CPUs do not automatically mean that eight worker threads will produce the best performance.

Performance depends on several factors:

  • Whether the task is CPU-intensive or I/O-intensive.
  • How much memory each worker requires.
  • How much work is involved in creating and communicating with workers.
  • Whether other applications are competing for CPU resources.
  • Whether the application runs inside a container with CPU restrictions.

The operating system schedules threads across available processors. Multiple threads can exist even when fewer processors are available, but excess runnable threads may compete for CPU time.

Therefore, CPU count is a useful starting point for selecting a worker count, not a universal rule for determining the optimal number of workers.

3. Four Strategies for Dividing Work

There is no single strategy that fits every workload. The right approach depends on the shape of the data and the amount of computation involved.

Strategy 1: Divide work based on CPU availability

For CPU-heavy calculations, the number of available logical CPUs is a reasonable starting point.

Node.js provides os.availableParallelism() to estimate how much CPU parallelism the process can use.

const os = require("node:os");

const availableCPUs = os.availableParallelism();

const workerCount = Math.max(1, availableCPUs - 1);

console.log("Available CPU parallelism:", availableCPUs);
console.log("Initial worker count:", workerCount);

On a machine reporting eight available logical CPUs, this example starts with seven workers.

Leaving capacity for the main thread can be useful, but it is not always necessary or optimal. The main thread might perform very little CPU work, or the application might run alongside other services that require substantial resources.

Benchmarking should determine the final worker count.

Strategy 2: Divide work based on data size

Suppose an application needs to process one million records using four workers.

A straightforward approach assigns approximately 250,000 records to each worker.

The general formula is:

chunkSize = ceil(totalItems / workerCount)

This approach is known as static partitioning because the work is divided before processing begins.

It works particularly well when each item requires roughly the same amount of computation.

However, equal numbers of records do not always mean equal amounts of work. For example, processing a record with two fields may take far less time than processing one containing a large nested object.

When processing costs vary significantly, static partitioning can leave some workers idle while others continue working.

Strategy 3: Divide work into smaller tasks

Instead of assigning one large block to each worker, an application can divide the workload into smaller jobs.

For example, rather than assigning 250,000 records to each worker, it could create batches of 10,000 records.

Workers retrieve additional batches as they finish their current tasks.

This is dynamic scheduling.

It is particularly useful when:

  • Tasks have unpredictable execution times.
  • Records vary in complexity.
  • Some jobs occasionally fail or need retries.
  • The application processes a continuous stream of incoming work.

Dynamic scheduling introduces additional overhead for managing the task queue, so the batches should not be so small that coordination becomes more expensive than the computation.

Strategy 4: Divide work based on resource limits

CPU availability is only one constraint. Memory can become the limiting factor.

Suppose every worker needs 500 MB of additional memory for its data and intermediate calculations. Creating 20 workers could require roughly 10 GB of additional memory, before accounting for the main application, runtime overhead, and other processes.

A practical worker system should consider:

  • CPU availability.
  • Memory available to the process.
  • Input and output data size.
  • Queue length.
  • Task duration.
  • Other application activity.

Resource-aware scheduling is especially important in production services and containerized environments.

4. A Complete Example: Distributing Work Across Node.js Workers

Let's build a working example that calculates the sum of all integers from 1 to 100 million.

The goal is to divide the calculation into separate ranges, assign each range to a worker, and combine the results.

Project structure 

parallel-calculation/
├── main.js
└── worker.js

Step 1: Create the worker

Create worker.js:

const {
  parentPort,
  workerData
} = require("node:worker_threads");

const { start, end } = workerData;

let sum = 0;

for (let i = start; i <= end; i++) {
  sum += i;
}

parentPort.postMessage(sum);

Each worker receives a start and end value, calculates the sum of its assigned range, and sends the result back to the main thread.

Step 2: Create the main program

Create main.js:

const os = require("node:os");

const {
  Worker
} = require("node:worker_threads");

const TOTAL = 100_000_000;

const availableCPUs = os.availableParallelism();

// Choose a starting worker count
const workerCount = Math.max(1, availableCPUs - 1);

const chunkSize = Math.ceil(TOTAL / workerCount);

function runWorker(start, end) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const worker = new Worker("./worker.js", {
      workerData: { start, end }
    });

    worker.once("message", resolve);
    worker.once("error", reject);

    worker.once("exit", (code) => {
      if (code !== 0) {
        reject(
          new Error(`Worker exited with code ${code}`)
        );
      }
    });
  });
}

async function main() {
  console.log("Available CPUs:", availableCPUs);
  console.log("Workers:", workerCount);

  const jobs = [];

  for (let i = 0; i < workerCount; i++) {
    const start = i * chunkSize + 1;

    const end = Math.min(
      (i + 1) * chunkSize,
      TOTAL
    );

    if (start <= end) {
      console.log(`Assigning range ${start}-${end}`);

      jobs.push(runWorker(start, end));
    }
  }

  const results = await Promise.all(jobs);

  const totalSum = results.reduce(
    (total, result) => total + result,
    0
  );

  console.log("Final sum:", totalSum);
}

main().catch(console.error);

Step 3: Run the program

Install Node.js if necessary, then run:

node main.js

The program detects available CPU parallelism, calculates a chunk size, launches workers, and waits for all results.

The expected result is:

Final sum: 5000000050000000

The output also displays the CPU count, worker count, and assigned ranges.

This example demonstrates the essential workflow:

  1. Detect available CPU parallelism.
  2. Determine the worker count.
  3. Divide the input into ranges.
  4. Run the calculations in separate threads.
  5. Collect the results.
  6. Combine the partial results.

For this particular arithmetic problem, a direct mathematical formula would be much faster than either implementation. The example is intended to demonstrate work partitioning, not to suggest that creating workers is always the fastest solution.

5. Static Partitioning vs. Dynamic Scheduling

The previous example uses static partitioning: each worker receives a predetermined range.

Consider a different scenario where an application processes customer analytics events. Some events contain simple properties, while others require expensive transformations.

Assigning the same number of events to every worker might not produce balanced execution times.

A dynamic task queue can solve this problem.

Conceptually, the system works like this:

Incoming tasks
      |
      v
    Queue
   /  |  \
  v   v   v
 W1  W2  W3
  |   |   |
  +---+---+
      |
      v
  Completed results

Whenever a worker finishes its current task, it takes another task from the queue.

This approach is often called work sharing. It can improve utilization when task durations vary, although the queue itself must be designed to avoid becoming a bottleneck.

A production implementation might also include retry policies, cancellation, timeouts, task priorities, and backpressure to prevent incoming work from exceeding processing capacity.

6. Why Worker Pools Are Better Than Creating a Thread for Every Task

Creating a worker involves initialization, communication setup, and resource allocation. If an application creates a new worker for every small task, this overhead can become significant.

A worker pool keeps a fixed number of workers alive and reuses them for multiple tasks.

For example, a pool might maintain four workers:

Worker pool
├── Worker 1 → Task A → Task E
├── Worker 2 → Task B → Task F
├── Worker 3 → Task C → Task G
└── Worker 4 → Task D → Task H

Tasks can wait in a queue until a worker becomes available.

A worker pool can provide:

  • Controlled concurrency.
  • Reduced worker initialization overhead.
  • More predictable resource usage.
  • Centralized error handling.
  • Better throughput for repeated CPU-heavy jobs.

In Node.js, worker pools can be implemented using worker_threads or libraries such as Piscina.

The pool size should still be selected according to the workload and measured performance.

7. How to Find the Optimal Number of Workers

Suppose a workload runs on a machine reporting eight available logical CPUs.

You could benchmark it using different worker counts:

Worker count What to evaluate
1 Baseline performance
2 Benefit from initial parallelism
4 Throughput and CPU utilization
6 Additional scaling
7 Potential balance with main-thread work
8 Whether using all available parallelism helps

Measure the time required to complete the same workload, as well as throughput, CPU utilization, memory usage, and latency.

For a CPU-intensive task, adding workers can reduce execution time until the workload becomes limited by processor capacity, memory bandwidth, synchronization, or other overhead.

Beyond that point, additional workers may offer little improvement or even reduce performance.

Also remember that worker threads are not independent physical CPUs. They share the machine's underlying resources, and CPU scheduling can affect their performance.

The best configuration is the one that meets your performance goals within your resource budget.

8. Common Mistakes to Avoid

Creating too many workers

More workers do not always mean faster execution. Excessive concurrency can increase memory consumption and scheduling overhead.

Assuming every task takes the same time

Equal-sized chunks work best when processing costs are reasonably uniform. For uneven tasks, dynamic scheduling can improve load balancing.

Using workers for ordinary I/O operations

Network requests and many file operations can already be handled asynchronously by Node.js. Workers are most valuable when substantial CPU-intensive JavaScript work would otherwise block the main thread.

Ignoring data-transfer costs

Workers normally communicate using messages, which can involve copying data. Large data transfers can offset the benefits of parallel computation. Transferable objects and shared memory can help in appropriate cases, but they require careful ownership and synchronization.

Ignoring memory limits

Every worker adds runtime overhead and may allocate its own data. A worker count that works on a development laptop might be inappropriate in a production container with less memory or CPU capacity.

9. Final Architecture: A Resource-Aware Worker System

For a production application, a robust design generally combines several of these techniques:

  1. Detect the available CPU parallelism.
  2. Establish a configurable upper limit for workers.
  3. Estimate the memory and processing cost of tasks.
  4. Divide work into appropriately sized batches.
  5. Use a worker pool to reuse threads.
  6. Use dynamic scheduling when tasks vary significantly in duration.
  7. Measure throughput, latency, CPU usage, and memory consumption.
  8. Adjust the configuration based on observed performance.

The result is a system that distributes work according to both the machine's capabilities and the workload's characteristics.

Conclusion

Multithreading is not just about creating more threads. It is about distributing work efficiently across the resources available to your application.

CPU-based partitioning provides a useful starting point. Data partitioning works well for uniform workloads. Dynamic scheduling helps balance uneven tasks, while resource-aware limits prevent excessive CPU and memory consumption.

For JavaScript developers, Node.js worker_threads provides the foundation for parallel CPU-intensive execution. Combining it with chunking, worker pools, and performance measurement can turn a single-threaded bottleneck into a more scalable processing system.

The key principle is simple: choose the worker count based on available resources, divide work according to its computational cost, and let real performance measurements guide optimization.

articles.title: I'm 13. I Built a Free Calorie Tracker That Shows You the Math. No Card, No Trial, No Paywall.
