articles.body_html:
I built a calorie tracker. It's called ForkCount. It's free. There's no card, no trial, no "start your 7-day free trial" wall, and no premium tier hiding the barcode scanner behind $12.99/month.

I'm 13. I can't write JavaScript from memory. I built it using Google AI Studio — describing what I wanted, testing what came back, fixing what broke. Two weeks of debugging. It's live now.

What it does

Shows you the math. Most apps give you a number. ForkCount gives you the number and the formula behind it — your BMR, your TDEE, your activity multiplier, your goal adjustment. Every step is visible. If you want to know why your target is 1,400 and not 2,000, the app tells you.

Calculates from your body, not an average. Mifflin-St Jeor for BMR, Katch-McArdle if you know your body fat percentage. Then activity level, then goal. The target is yours, not a default.

Logs food by typing. "200g chicken and 150g rice" parses to two items with macros. No searching a database for each ingredient. Type it, log it.

Weekly meal plans that use your target. Not a generic 2000 kcal plan. Your calorie target. Your dietary preference. If you're vegetarian, the plan is vegetarian.

Tracks water, weight, and exercise. Water in glasses, weight in trends, exercise with kcal burned.

Runs in your phone browser. No download. No app store. Open the link, sign up, done.

What it doesn't do

  • No food photo scan (in progress)
  • No barcode scanner (removed after it kept misfiring — it's coming back when it works)
  • No Apple Health / Google Fit sync
  • No verified nutrition data for anything not in the built-in list
  • No premium tier, because there's no business model. It's just free.

Why I built it

Every calorie app I tried wanted a card before it showed me anything useful. The math was always hidden. The target was always a black box. The "free" version was always a trial, or an ad-supported version of a paid app, or a version that locked the one feature you actually needed behind a subscription.

So I built one that doesn't do that. The math is visible. The target is yours. The app is free.

Why I'm posting

I want to know if the calorie math is right. If you've tracked long enough to know your real TDEE, run the onboarding and compare. If the number ForkCount gives you is off by more than 100 kcal, tell me how and I'll fix it. If it's right, tell me that too — I need to know the calculator works before I trust it.

I also want to know what's missing. What feature do you use in MyFitnessPal that you can't live without? What would make you switch? Not "add every feature" — what's the one thing?

Try it

https://forkcount.github.io

Free. No card. No trial. Works on any phone browser. Two weeks old, so there will be bugs — but every bug I hear about gets fixed within a day.

If you try it and something breaks, tell me what you were doing and what phone you're on. I read every message.

Built with React, Vite, Supabase, and a lot of patience. Deployed on GitHub Pages. If you're building something similar and want to know how the Supabase migration went, ask in the comments — I'll write it up.

articles.title: I tested my browser-based email checkers against dkimpy, checkdmarc and pyspf: 12,618 results, 76 disagreements
articles.description: Five email security tools that run in the browser (DKIM, DMARC, SPF, MX and header analysis), each benchmarked against the Python library people already trust. Where we disagreed, who was right, and the bug the benchmark caught.
articles.body_html:
I built five email security tools for Toggle9 that run in the browser: a DKIM checker, a DMARC checker, an SPF checker, an MX lookup and an email header analyzer. There's no backend. DNS queries go from your browser to Cloudflare's public resolver, and DKIM signatures are verified with WebCrypto.

That raises an obvious question: why would anyone trust a JavaScript reimplementation of RFC 6376? There are established open-source libraries for all of this: dkimpy for DKIM, checkdmarc for DMARC and MX, pyspf (the reference implementation of RFC 7208) for SPF, and mail-parser for headers.

So I ran each tool against one of them, on real data, and read every result where they disagreed.

The scoreboard

Tool Reference Test set Compared Same answer
DKIM checker dkimpy 1.1.8 510 real emails from 18 public mailing lists 623 signatures 623
Email header analyzer mail-parser 4.8.0 The same 510 emails 2,333 hops 2,333
DMARC checker checkdmarc 5.17.2 747 popular domains (Tranco top 500 + top 250 .uk) 705 domains 692 (98.2%)
SPF checker pyspf 2.0.14 The first 200 of those domains that publish SPF 454 IP checks 451
MX lookup checkdmarc 5.17.2 746 domains 8,503 checks 8,443

That's 12,618 results and 76 disagreements. The benchmarks ran on 22 and 23 October 2026. The rest of this post is about those 76.

How a browser does DNS

Every tool here needs DNS: TXT records for SPF, DMARC and DKIM keys, MX records, and TLSA and PTR records. Browsers can't send raw DNS queries, but they can use DNS over HTTPS. Cloudflare's resolver answers JSON:

const r = await fetch(`https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query?name=${encodeURIComponent(name)}&type=${type}`, {
  headers: { accept: 'application/dns-json' },
  referrerPolicy: 'no-referrer',
  credentials: 'omit',
});
const j = await r.json();
// j.Status: 0 = NOERROR, 3 = NXDOMAIN. j.Answer: [{ name, type, TTL, data }]

The real resolver adds a cache per check, a limit of six queries in flight, a 6-second timeout and one retry. An SPF check can fan out into dozens of lookups, so the cache matters more than you'd expect.

For DMARC, SPF and MX, my tools and the reference libraries queried the same resolver (1.1.1.1), so a difference can't be blamed on two resolvers seeing different DNS.

DKIM: 623 of 623, and why 65 signatures "failed"

DKIM verification is canonicalization (RFC 6376 section 3.4), then a hash, then a signature check. The relaxed header rule fits in a few lines:

export function canonHeader(raw, how) {
  if (how === 'simple') return raw + '\r\n';
  const i = raw.indexOf(':');
  const name = raw.slice(0, i).replace(/[ \t]+$/, '').toLowerCase();
  const val = raw.slice(i + 1).replace(/\r\n(?=[ \t])/g, '').replace(/[ \t]+/g, ' ').replace(/^ | $/g, '');
  return `${name}:${val}\r\n`;
}

WebCrypto handles both DKIM signing algorithms, RSA and Ed25519 (simplified):

if (alg === 'ed25519-sha256')
  return crypto.subtle.importKey('raw', pubKey, { name: 'Ed25519' }, false, ['verify']);
return crypto.subtle.importKey('spki', spki, { name: 'RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5', hash: 'SHA-256' }, false, ['verify']);

The test set was 510 recent posts to 18 public mailing lists, taken from lore.kernel.org's public git mirrors. They had 623 signatures from 57 domains; two of the signatures used Ed25519. dkimpy and my checker gave the same pass or fail on all 623.

The useful part was the 65 signatures that failed in both. A checker that just says "fail" isn't much help, so mine reads the receiving server's own Authentication-Results header (RFC 8601) to work out when the email changed:

  • 62 had passed when the email arrived, according to the receiving server. They were changed afterwards. In 60 of them, a signed List-Unsubscribe header was missing: the archive removes it before it publishes the email.
  • 3 had already failed on arrival. They were changed on the way.

So most of the "broken DKIM" in that set wasn't broken at delivery. It's what an archive does to an email. That's the line the tool shows: "The email was fine when it was delivered."

Email headers: 2,333 of 2,333

The header analyzer turns Received: headers into a route: which server handed the email to which, when, and how long each hop took. mail-parser parses the same headers. On the same 510 emails, both found the same number of hops in every email, and all 2,333 hops matched on server, time and delay.

DMARC: the benchmark caught my bug

The first DMARC run agreed on everything for 682 of 705 domains (96.7%). I read every difference, and the biggest group was mine to fix.

My checker called it an error when an SPF record reached the same include: from two branches. msn.com, doi.org, grammarly.com and 7 others do this. I'd treated a repeat as a loop. Nothing in RFC 7208 makes a repeated include an error. Real loops get caught by the 10-lookup limit, and a repeat just counts against that limit. The fix: follow the repeat, count it again, and show a warning.

The second run agreed on 692 of 705 (98.2%). I read the 13 that were left by hand, against the RFCs:

Domains What happened Who's right
www.gov.uk, legislation.gov.uk, account.gov.uk, data.gov.uk No DMARC record of their own. The parent gov.uk record's sp=none applies to subdomains (RFC 9989). Mine
gcdn.co, thomsonreuters.co.uk SPF includes a name that doesn't exist in DNS, which is a permerror (RFC 7208 section 5.2) Mine
weather.com An unrelated TXT record at _dmarc alongside the real one; checkdmarc rejects it Mine
autodesk.com An = in the local part of a ruf address, which the standard allows Mine
alibabadns.com v=SPF1 in capitals. The ABNF is case-insensitive. Mine
globo.com rua=mailto: dmarc@… with a space. Both call the address invalid; checkdmarc then rejects the whole record, but RFC 9989 keeps p=none. Mine
iiko.it, who.int 15 and 17 DNS lookups (iiko.it confirmed by hand through 1.1.1.1). checkdmarc stops counting early. Mine
ozon.ru checkdmarc timed out Neither

"Mine" is my reading of the standards, written up with the RFC section each time. You don't have to take my word for it: the domains are real, so you can check them.

None of this makes checkdmarc a bad library. Rejecting a record the standards would accept is a reasonable choice for a tool that audits your own domain. Mine follows the standards' wording, because its job is to explain what a receiver should do with the record.

SPF: 451 of 454, and the 3 that weren't real

For each of 200 domains, I tested up to four IP addresses: the domain's own mail server, an address inside a range its record lists, an address reserved for documentation that never sends email, and a Google sending address for domains that include Google.

Three results differed: youtube.com, archive.org and youtube-nocookie.com, all for the same Google address. Large providers' DNS answers rotate, so an address can be listed in one lookup and missing from the next. Run again side by side, both tools agreed on all three.

MX: 8,443 of 8,503, and the rotation problem

The MX lookup checks a lot per domain: the MX hosts, their addresses, reverse DNS (PTR) and whether it points back, TLSA (DANE) records, MTA-STS and TLS reporting. Across 746 domains that came to 8,503 comparisons.

MX host sets matched on all 746 domains. MTA-STS and TLS reporting matched on all 746 too.

The addresses were the hard part. 738 of the 1,246 mail servers answered with a different few of their addresses each time. Google, Microsoft and Proofpoint spread their load that way, so two lookups a few minutes apart rarely agree, from any tool. Comparing those sets directly would only measure luck.

So the benchmark asks each server again over a few seconds. If those lookups turn up every address either tool saw, the server counts as rotating and isn't compared. That left 508 servers with steady answers, and 458 matched exactly. Of the 50 that didn't, 47 are Google or Proofpoint servers of the same rotating kind, whose other address didn't turn up in those few seconds.

The remaining 10 were differences in records. On 26 October I checked each one by hand through 1.1.1.1. In every case, the record my tool found is there:

  • TLSA: mx.ietf.org, two comcast.net servers and cm.com's Microsoft server publish TLSA records. checkdmarc reported none.
  • PTR: three servers (nic.ru, debian.org, ebi.ac.uk) have reverse DNS. checkdmarc reported none.
  • Forward-confirmed PTR: two huawei.com names do resolve back to their addresses.
  • Addresses: one Outlook server has IPv6 addresses that checkdmarc didn't list.

What I'd tell anyone writing a benchmark like this

  1. A reference library is a witness, not a judge. If you count disagreements as your failures, you end up copying the library's choices. Read each one against the spec.
  2. Read every difference, especially at the start. My first DMARC run had a real bug hiding behind a 96.7% score that looked fine.
  3. Handle rotating answers before comparing. Otherwise you're measuring DNS load balancing, not your code.
  4. Tie the results to the code. Each tool's test file hashes its engine and compares that with the hash stored in its benchmark result. Change the DKIM verifier without re-running the benchmark, and npm test fails: 
test('dkim-bench.json was made by the engine that ships', () => {
  const b = JSON.parse(readFileSync(new URL('dkim-bench.json', dir), 'utf8'));
  const h = createHash('sha256')
    .update(readFileSync(new URL('verify.js', dir)))
    .update(readFileSync(new URL('compute.js', dir)))
    .digest('hex').slice(0, 16);
  assert.equal(b.engine, h);
});

So the numbers quoted on each tool's page can't silently drift away from the code.

Try them

All five run in your browser, with no account. When you check a domain, only the DNS names go to Cloudflare's public resolver. Headers and emails you paste are read on your device.

  • DKIM checker
  • DMARC checker
  • SPF checker
  • MX lookup
  • Email header analyzer

If you check DMARC for a living, I'd like to hear where you think I've read RFC 9989 wrong, especially on those 13.

articles.title: I got tired of reading CSS bugs in a tiny overlay, so I made my debugger print a report
articles.description: BeeLadybug, my open-source debug overlay, has always shown what's happening in real time: FPS, logs,...
articles.body_html:
BeeLadybug, my open-source debug overlay, has always shown what's happening in real time: FPS, logs, !important, z-index traps, clicks being swallowed by the wrong element.

The problem is the overlay. Make it big and it covers the game or the page you're debugging. Make it small, the way it is now, and you're squinting at a phone-sized box on the left of the screen while the rows scroll past.

One evening I gave up and asked myself a simple question: why can't I just press a key and get everything on one page, to read calmly?

One key, one file

Version 0.6.1 adds exportReport(). Press F8, or the EXPORT button, and you get report-YYYYMMDD-HHMM.html:

  • a summary at the top: errors, warnings, ok
  • the Core log with sim time and frame
  • series: FPS min / avg / max, nodes, mutations
  • one section per adapter: Canvas hitboxes and collisions, DOM box model and clipped nodes, CSS (!important, stacking contexts, intercepted clicks, overflow), long tasks, slow resources, Python metrics

It's plain HTML with a dark theme. Ctrl+P turns it into a PDF. You can also get json (for CI or an AI agent) or csv (for a spreadsheet).

import { BeeLadybugCore, exportReport } from 'bee-ladybug';

const bee = new BeeLadybugCore();
// ...attach adapters...
exportReport(bee, { format: 'html' }); // downloads the file

In headless mode (ui: false) nothing is downloaded. The function just returns the data, so it works in Node and in bots too.

How it fits a "blind" Core

The Core still knows nothing about Canvas, the DOM or Python. Each adapter can now register an optional snapshot() hook that returns rows like { severity, selector, rule, value, source }. The exporter asks every registered adapter for its snapshot, and if one throws, it becomes a single warn row while the rest of the report still renders. A new adapter only has to implement snapshot() to show up in the report.

Then I pointed it at real sites

First, my own games portal. It found:

  • my .entry-content creating a stacking context that traps the z-index of the game grid
  • a container blocking clicks on three elements
  • an average of 33 FPS, which explains a lot

Then, for fun, a big professional games portal. 25 errors, 51 warnings 😄 To be fair, most of them are intentional tricks: negative margins so a carousel can bleed to the edges, and content clipped on purpose inside cards. Their site works great. It still averaged ~52 FPS with 3× my DOM nodes, which taught me more than the error count did.

…and it found bugs in itself

The best part of testing on real pages: the report exposed its own weak spots.

  • an icon from the WordPress admin bar slipped through the filter
  • the same row repeated dozens of times instead of being grouped as ×N
  • the summary said "0 errors" while the log had four of them

All three are being fixed. A debugger that finds bugs in itself on its first real run felt like a good sign.

Try it

Install it in your project:

npm i bee-ladybug

Or try it right now without installing: open any page, press F12 and paste this in the console, then press F8 for the report.

import('https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bee-ladybug@0.6.1/src/index.js')
  .then(({ BeeLadybugCore, WebDOMAdapter, CSSAdapter }) => {
    const bee = new BeeLadybugCore();
    new WebDOMAdapter(bee, { root: document.body }).attach();
    new CSSAdapter(bee).attach();
    window.bee = bee;
  });

Feedback welcome, especially from people debugging Canvas games and DOM-heavy pages.

articles.title: FableCut Gets its Own Studio Which Agents Can Actually Use
articles.description: I've been building FableCut for the past few months, and one thing I've wanted to explore is what...
articles.body_html:
I've been building FableCut for the past few months, and one thing I've wanted to explore is what video editing looks like when an AI agent can work directly with the editor instead of just generating instructions for a human to follow.

The idea is straightforward: open a video editor, connect an AI agent, describe the edit you want, and let the agent make changes to your actual project.

That project is now FableCut Studio.

Studio: https://studio.fablecut.space/

GitHub: https://github.com/ronak-create/FableCut

Here's a quick demo of FableCut Studio in action:

What is FableCut?

FableCut is an open-source video editor designed to work with AI agents through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

The project started as a local editor that agents could control through project.json and MCP. The first version shipped on July 6, 2026.

Since then, I've shipped 20 tagged versions, made 383 commits, and grown the project to 747 GitHub stars and 86 forks. It's available on npm as fablecut, is listed in the official MCP registry, and has been included in awesome-mcp-servers.

The original version required a local installation. Studio takes the same idea into the browser.

You open a link, load a project, connect an agent, and start editing.

No editor installation is required.

Why let an AI agent control a video editor?

Most AI video tools focus on generating a new video from a prompt. I wanted to explore something different: letting an agent work with an existing editing timeline.

Imagine giving an agent instructions like:

  • Cut every occurrence of "you know" from this recording.
  • Caption this reel in a highlight style.
  • Remove the pauses from this take.
  • Adjust the color grading of this shot.
  • Export the final video in a vertical format.

These tasks involve more than generating a video. The agent needs to understand the project, make targeted changes, and preserve the existing work.

That's the direction I've been building toward with FableCut.

How Studio works

Studio runs at https://studio.fablecut.space/ and exposes 16 tools through remote MCP.

Different clients can connect to it, including Claude Code, claude.ai, Cursor, ChatGPT, OpenCode, and other compatible MCP clients.

The connection process depends on the client. For example, claude.ai supports a custom connector, while Claude Code can connect using a command.

Once connected, the agent can call tools to inspect and modify the project. Those changes appear live in the editor.

There's also an Agent panel that lists tool calls, and you can pause the agent or issue a new link when needed.

The important part is that the agent isn't simply returning a list of suggestions. It's interacting with the actual editing project.

What happens to the files?

In Chromium-based browsers such as Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Arc, Studio can work with a folder on your disk and save project.json there.

Firefox and Safari use browser storage for projects, with a download option for exporting the project as a ZIP.

Your video clips are not uploaded to Studio's server.

There is one important distinction: the remote MCP relay carries tool calls and their results, including project information and any frames the agent requests. It does not receive the media files themselves.

I think being clear about this boundary matters when building AI tools that work with local files.

What's new in v1.17?

The latest release adds transcription and text-based editing to Studio.

These features make it possible to perform common editing tasks using the words spoken in a video rather than manually searching through the timeline.

1. Transcription directly in the browser

Studio uses Whisper to transcribe audio in the browser.

The model is approximately 77 MB and downloads the first time transcription is used. After that initial download, transcription runs on the device.

In one desktop CPU test, 48 seconds of speech took 13 seconds to transcribe.

That is a useful result for a feature that doesn't require uploading the audio to a transcription service.

2. Editing videos through text

Once a transcript is available, you can interact with the words directly.

You can click a word to jump to its position, select words and delete them, or search for a phrase and cut every occurrence in one operation.

The cuts are grouped into a single undo step, making it easier to experiment without losing control of the edit.

For example, if a recording contains several repetitions of the same phrase, you can remove those repetitions without manually locating each one on the timeline.

3. Word-by-word captions

Studio can generate captions from the transcript and time them word by word.

The available styles include:

  • Subtitle
  • Karaoke
  • Highlight, where the currently spoken word changes color
  • Word pop

Caption layouts also adapt to the canvas dimensions, so vertical videos can use narrower lines than landscape videos.

SRT and VTT import and export are supported as well.

4. Silence removal

Studio can automatically remove pauses from a recording.

This is useful for talking-head videos, tutorials, interviews, and short-form content where long pauses can make the final video feel slow.

One limitation worth mentioning: Whisper generally drops filler words such as "um" and "uh". Silence removal and transcript-based editing serve different purposes, so filler removal is better handled through the silence-removal workflow rather than assuming every filler will appear in the transcript.

5. Agents can use these features too

The transcription and editing features aren't limited to manual use in the browser.

Agents can use tools such as fablecut_transcribe, fablecut_captions, and fablecut_silence.

That means a prompt like "caption this reel in highlight style" can become an actual editing operation instead of a tutorial explaining how to create captions.

This is where I think MCP becomes particularly useful: it gives an agent a structured way to interact with an existing application.

There's more than speech editing

The project has grown well beyond basic timeline operations.

Over the last several releases, I've added:

  • Advanced editing: source monitoring, ripple and roll edits, track targeting, markers, and typed timecode.
  • Audio tools: mixer buses, effect chains, automation, loudness normalization, auto-ducking, crossfades, and noise reduction.
  • Color grading: waveform monitoring, RGB parade, vectorscopes, color wheels, curves, and HSL adjustments.
  • Compositing: masks, track mattes, and motion tracking.
  • Motion graphics: shape layers, parenting, motion paths, motion blur, text on a path, and animation presets.
  • Media management: metadata search, offline relinking, proxies, delivery presets, and batch export.
  • Project management: multiple sequences, version history, and faster exports through WebCodecs.

These features matter because an agent needs a real editing environment to work with. The more capable the editor becomes, the more useful its tools can be.

Agents can also inspect frames, measure color grades using scopes, and save project versions before substantial edits. The editor respects track locks rather than treating the entire timeline as freely editable.

Exporting without sending your video to a server

Studio encodes exports in the browser, supporting formats and codecs including H.264, HEVC, VP9, and AV1, with supported audio options.

WebCodecs has also helped make exports substantially faster. In v1.16, the project introduced an export path measured at roughly five times faster than the previous implementation.

For an editing application, performance matters just as much as the AI integration. An agent might make the right changes, but the workflow is still frustrating if exporting the result takes too long.

What if you prefer running everything locally?

Studio isn't the only way to use FableCut.

You can install the local version through npm:

npx -y fablecut

The local version exposes 21 MCP tools and supports additional machine-local workflows, including FFmpeg-dependent features.

This is a useful option if you prefer a local agent setup or need functionality that isn't available in the browser version.

Try it yourself

I've added a demo project containing skate clips, a music track, and an initial edit. You don't need to prepare your own footage just to see how the editor works.

  1. Open FableCut Studio.
  2. Load the demo project.
  3. Connect a compatible AI agent.
  4. Try asking it to caption the video or remove pauses.

You can also explore the source code on GitHub.

FableCut is released under the MIT license.

What's next?

I'm continuing to build FableCut around the idea that AI agents should be able to work inside real creative applications, with structured tools and visible results.

There's still plenty to improve, but the latest release brings the project closer to a workflow where an agent can help with the tedious parts of editing while the editor remains the place where the actual project lives.

If you try it, I'd genuinely like to hear what works, what breaks, and what you'd want an agent to be able to do next.
